items.title: Israeli military completes ground operation in Gaza beyond Yellow Line
items.summary: Hamas condemned the incursion, which the Israeli military said was to dismantle a "terror tunnel", as a "flagrant" ceasefire violation.
items.body:
Image source, Reuters

Image caption,

Residents fled the area near Nuseirat and Bureij refugee camps following the Israeli evacuation order

ByDavid Gritten

Israeli ground forces have launched a rare operation in part of the central Gaza Strip outside their control, after issuing evacuation orders for residents.

Witnesses said tanks advanced east of Nuseirat refugee camp and rolled onto the territory's main north to south road under the cover of artillery strikes.

The Israeli military said the "targeted" operation aimed to dismantle a "terror tunnel" west of the so-called Yellow Line, which marks the more than 60% of Gaza's territory occupied by Israel.

The Palestinian armed group Hamas, which controls the rest of Gaza, accused Israel of a "flagrant violation" of the October 2025 ceasefire agreement.

Violence has continued in Gaza over the past 13 months, with near-daily Israeli strikes, and living conditions for the 2.1 million people there remain dire.

Early on Wednesday afternoon, Israeli military body Cogat's Arabic spokesperson announced the start of the incursion and warned Palestinians living in an area north of Nuseirat and Bureij refugee camp to stay away for their own safety.

It also said a section of the north to south Salah al-Din road that passed through the area would be closed to traffic.

Later, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said it had begun a joint operation with the Shin Bet security service "to dismantle a terror tunnel west of the Yellow Line that posed an immediate and direct threat to IDF troops".

"IDF troops under the Southern Command are deployed in the area in accordance with the ceasefire agreement and will continue to operate to remove any immediate threat and thwart attempts by the Hamas terrorist organisation to harm Israeli civilians or IDF troops, or to violate the agreement," it added.

Hamas warned in a statement that the advance of Israeli military vehicles beyond the Yellow Line and the evacuation of residents constituted "a dangerous development and a flagrant violation of the ceasefire agreement".

Footage published by Palestinian media outlets and on social media showed families fleeing areas near Nuseirat camp following the announcement.

In one video verified by BBC Verify, a man can be seen ducking after hearing artillery fire and then running along Salah al-Din road, about 1.5km (0.9 miles) west of the Yellow Line. "The Israeli occupation now is firing randomly near the houses and tents of people," he says.

Automatic gunfire can be heard in another video filmed just to the south-east.

A resident of Nuseirat who was forced to flee told BBC Arabic's Middle East Daily programme: "The situation is now extremely dire, with Israeli forces firing indiscriminately at areas where displaced people have sought shelter."

"We couldn't take any of our belongings with us - not even our blankets, pillows, or clothes. We had no choice but to leave everything behind."

A second resident also reported "indiscriminate gunfire and shelling" and said there had been "numerous casualties, including fatalities".

Asked about reported fatalities, the IDF sent a general statement about the operation.

Gaza's Hamas-run Civil Defence agency said three people were killed and others were wounded in three separate Israeli drone strikes on Wednesday.

One man was killed in Nuseirat, the second to the north in Gaza City, and the third in the central town of Deir al-Balah, it added.

The Israeli military said the first two strikes targeted "terrorists" and that it was not aware of the third incident, according to AFP news agency.

At least 1,658 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza since the ceasefire began last year, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

The Israeli military says six of its soldiers have been killed over the same period.

Meanwhile, more than 1.9 million people - about 90% of Gaza's population - remain displaced, with 1.4 million of them living in tents or makeshift shelters, according to the UN.

Reconstruction has yet to begin in Gaza, where an estimated 82% of all structures have been destroyed or damaged during the war, as US President Donald Trump's peace plan has largely stalled.

The disarmament of Hamas has been a key sticking point.

The group has agreed to give up its weapons in exchange for a phased withdrawal of Israeli troops from the 60% of Gaza they currently occupy. But Israel has insisted that Hamas must fully disarm before any pullout.

The war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.

Since then, more than 74,700 people have been killed in Gaza, the health ministry says.

blocks.text: 图片来源：Reuters
图片说明，
在以色列发出撤离命令后，居民逃离了努塞拉特和布雷吉难民营附近地区
作者：David Gritten
在向居民发出撤离命令后，以色列地面部队在其控制范围之外的加沙地带中部部分地区发动了一次罕见行动。
目击者称，坦克在炮火掩护下向努塞拉特难民营以东推进，并开上了该地区主要的南北向道路。
以色列军方表示，此次“定点”行动旨在拆除所谓“黄线”以西的一条“恐怖地道”；黄线标示以色列占领的加沙超过 60% 的领土。
控制加沙其余地区的巴勒斯坦武装组织哈马斯指责以色列“公然违反”2025 年 10 月的停火协议。
过去 13 个月里，加沙的暴力仍在持续，以色列几乎每天都在空袭，当地 210 万居民的生活条件依然极其恶劣。
周三下午早些时候，以色列军方机构 Cogat 的阿拉伯语发言人宣布开始此次突入，并警告居住在努塞拉特和布雷吉难民营以北地区的巴勒斯坦人，为自身安全起见不要靠近。
它还表示，穿过该地区、由北向南的一段萨拉赫丁路将对交通关闭。
随后，以色列国防军（IDF）表示，已与国内安全机构辛贝特（Shin Bet）开始联合行动，「以拆除黄线以西一条对以军构成即时直接威胁的恐怖地道」。
声明还称：“南部司令部所属以军部队根据停火协议部署在该地区，并将继续采取行动，消除任何直接威胁，挫败哈马斯恐怖组织伤害以色列平民或以军部队、或违反协议的企图。”
哈马斯在声明中警告称，以色列军车越过黄线推进以及疏散居民，构成“危险的事态发展，也是对停火协议的公然违反”。
巴勒斯坦媒体和社交媒体发布的画面显示，宣布之后，家人们正在逃离努塞拉特营地附近地区。
在一段经 BBC Verify 核实的视频中，可见一名男子在听到炮火后低头躲避，然后沿萨拉赫丁路奔跑，该处位于黄线以西约 1.5 公里（0.9 英里）。他说：“以色列占领军现在正在民房和帐篷附近随意开火。”
在另一段拍摄于东南方向不远处的视频中，可以听到自动武器开火声。
一名被迫逃离的努赛拉特居民告诉 BBC 阿拉伯语频道的《中东日报》节目：「现在的情况极其严峻，以色列部队正在对流离失所者寻求避难的地区进行不分青红皂白的射击。」
“我们什么随身物品都带不走——连毯子、枕头和衣服都不行。我们别无选择，只能把一切留下。”
另一位居民也报告称遭遇“不分青红皂白的枪击和炮击”，并说“已有多人伤亡，包括死亡”。
在被问及所报道的死亡人数时，以色列国防军只发了一份关于此次行动的笼统声明。
由哈马斯管理的加沙民防部门表示，周三在三次以色列无人机袭击中有三人死亡、多人受伤。
它补充说，一人在努塞拉特丧生，第二人在北面的加沙城，第三人在中部城镇戴尔拜莱赫。
据法新社报道，以色列军方称前两次袭击目标是“恐怖分子”，并表示不清楚第三次事件。
据该地区由哈马斯运作的卫生部门称，自去年停火开始以来，至少有1,658人在以色列对加沙的袭击中丧生，联合国认为这些数字是可靠的。
以色列军方表示，同期有六名士兵阵亡。
与此同时，据联合国称，仍有超过 190 万人——约占加沙人口的 90%——流离失所，其中 140 万人住在帐篷或临时住所中。
加沙的重建尚未开始，据估计战争期间约 82% 的建筑被摧毁或损坏，而美国总统 Donald Trump 的和平计划基本上陷入停滞。
哈马斯解除武装一直是关键症结。
该组织已同意放弃武器，以换取以色列军队从其目前占领的 60% 加沙地带分阶段撤出。但以色列坚持哈马斯必须先完全解除武装，才能开始任何撤军。
这场战争由哈马斯主导的 2023 年 10 月 7 日袭击以色列南部所引发，当时约有 1,200 人遇难，另有 251 人被劫为人质。
卫生部门表示，自那时起，加沙已有超过 74,700 人丧生。

items.summary: Experts say ‘insanely complex’ £100,000 limit proposed for overseas donors should be replaced by universal cap Andy Burnham is facing calls to commit to a cap on all political donations when the elections bill is in the House of Lords, instead of the “insanely complex” £100,000 limit on overseas don…
items.body:
Andy Burnham during prime minister’s questions this week. Photograph: House of Commons/PA

Andy Burnham during prime minister’s questions this week. Photograph: House of Commons/PA

Cap all political donations, not only those from overseas, Burnham told

Experts say ‘insanely complex’ £100,000 limit proposed for overseas donors should be replaced by universal cap

Andy Burnham is facing calls to commit to a cap on all political donations when the elections bill is in the House of Lords, instead of the “insanely complex” £100,000 limit on overseas donors. It is uncertain whether the £72m worth of donations recently received by Reform UK will be affected.

The Labour former home secretary David Blunkett is one of many peers to have tabled an amendment calling for an overall cap, proposing a £500,000 annual limit per donor, with his plan believed to have broad support.

Various amendments to the legislation, known officially as the representation of the people bill, are due to be debated in the House of Lords in the coming weeks, with proposals for a cap set at levels ranging from £1,000 to £5m a year.

What are the rules on political donations and gifts in the UK?

Read more

No 10 has previously promised to bring forward a taskforce that will look at the possibility of a wider donations cap as part of tackling mega-donations. However, sources say senior figures would prefer this to be brought forward in a new bill aimed at cleaning up politics in the next session of parliament, rather than holding up current legislation. Labour is also yet to overcome the opposition of unions worried that limits affecting their own ability to donate could water down their influence.

Before the Lords debate, experts are urging the government to replace the overseas cap with a blanket cap for all donors to avoid the numerous possible loopholes in the new law applying to donors based abroad.

The overseas donor cap was announced in March and is meant to apply from that point, meaning it could cover Reform’s £36m from crypto billionaire Ben Delo and a further £36m from Christopher Harborne donated this autumn.

However, Reform insists it will not have to hand back the money and will challenge its retrospective application in the courts, given the legislation has not yet passed.

Delo’s donation is less likely to be caught by the cap as he has long been registered to vote in the UK, but Harborne’s donation is more in contention because he has previously been an overseas elector and registered to vote in Britain only in June this year.

Nigel Farage, the leader of Reform UK. The party has said it will challenge any retrospective application of the elections bill in the courts. Photograph: Peter Nicholls/Getty Images

Some officials are worried about the prospect of a judicial review in relation to the retrospective aspect of the legislation, with the House of Lords constitution committee saying it “has not been sufficiently justified and would set an unwelcome precedent”.

However, government sources insist this element will go ahead, saying retrospective legislation is not a new concept and there are multiple precedents under successive administrations, particularly to address the risk of people taking action immediately to avoid the new rules.

New government amendments to the elections bill, aimed at tightening the overseas donor cap, bring in complicated rules around donations held in trusts and as loans, as well as requiring formal declarations about residency aimed at identifying which donations may have to be returned.

But Rose Zussman, a senior policy manager at Transparency International UK, said: “If a cap is right for donors living overseas, it’s right for all donors.”

She added: “These amendments concede that unlimited donations put our democracy at risk, but stop short of the obvious solution. Singling out one group of donors risks appearing partisan and makes already complex rules harder to follow. The simpler answer, and one the public overwhelmingly backs, is a universal cap on how much anyone can give to a political party.”

Susan Hawley, the director of Spotlight on Corruption, agreed that an overall donations cap would be simpler. “With almost 180 government amendments, this bill is now becoming insanely complex, which will make it extremely hard to navigate and enforce,” she said.

after newsletter promotion

“But it is also clear that the government is disregarding the mood of the country by sticking its head in the sand instead of taking steps to get big money and undue influence out of party political funding, by introducing a donation cap and spending limits.”

Stella Creasy, the Labour MP who proposed a £100,000 cap when the bill was in the Commons, said a separate piece of legislation for a cap would be too late.

Stella Creasy, the Labour MP who proposed the £100,000 limit on overseas donations. Photograph: PjrNews/Alamy

“If you are concerned about billionaires buying the next election, you have to stop it at the source,” she said. “You can’t wait until it’s been spent and then say that was too much. I have been taken aback at the strength of feeling in the House of Lords that we cannot let billionaires with UK postcodes define the next election.”

Despite Burnham’s previous support for a donation cap, trade unions have been pushing back against the idea over fears that a rightwing government could take steps to stop large donations from their movement in future.

Shaun Bowler, the founder of grassroots campaign WakeUpGB, who previously secured written support for a cap from Burnham before he became prime minister, said: “I approached Andy Burnham in good faith and welcomed his support for a donation cap. I genuinely believed he wanted to change the culture of Westminster.

“But when his government subsequently declined to back a general cap, I felt he had broken the pledge he made to me. Now parliament has a £1,000 proposal before it. I welcome that, but why should trade unions be exempt?

“Unions historically helped Labour counter wealthy Conservative donors. I understand that. But the answer isn’t to preserve enormous donations on either side. It is to introduce the same fair limit for everyone.”

items.summary: Meeting comes after Trump declared Putin a ‘friend’ during trilateral meeting with Xi in China For what it’s worth, the China-US-Russia ‘peace declaration’ issued after their meeting, and published by Chinese state media , includes absolutely no mention of Ukraine or Europe whatsoever. There is only…
items.body:
Poland’s prime minister Donald Tusk – one of Europe’s five negotiators – does not seem to be impressed by what he saw in Shenzhen.

“God, protect us from such friends,” he said on X in an apparent reference to Trump’s enthusiastic greeting with Putin.

Poland’s foreign minister Radosław Sikorski was similarly alarmed, telling reporters:

“Indeed, it is difficult to judge, by their fruits we shall know them, but the optics of this hugging Putin, calling him a friend, causes us some concern.
Because the question arises – who is he more of a friend with, Putin or our president? And what will he possibly do if push comes to shove, which friend will he choose?”

items.title: Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya minority, top UN court rules
items.summary: The unprecedented International Court of Justice verdict concerns a 2017 military crackdown that killed thousands.
items.body:
Figure caption,

Watch: Genocide judgement will 'mean a great deal' for Rohingya community

ByAleks Phillips, Anna Holligan, Reporting fromat The Hague, and Jonathan Head, South East Asia correspondent

Myanmar has been found guilty of committing genocide against its Rohingya minority by the International Court of Justice (ICJ).

The verdict marks the first time a state has ever been found to have committed genocide by an international court.

Yuji Iwasawa, president of the UN's top court, said Myanmar had the "intention to destroy" a substantial part of the Rohingya population and engaged in "extensive destruction of evidence" to hide its crimes.

A military crackdown in 2017 killed thousands of Rohingya and forced more than 700,000 to flee Buddhist-majority Myanmar, formerly known as Burma. Myanmar denied the claims against it, saying its forces had responded to attacks by armed groups.

The court found on Thursday that "genocidal intent is the only reasonable inference that can be drawn from the evidence" it had seen.

The verdict was reached by a majority of nine votes to six among a panel of judges from around the world. The ICJ also found in favour by majority that Myanmar had violated several other parts of the 1948 Genocide Convention.

The case brought by The Gambia centred around so-called "clearance operations" initiated in 2017 in Rakhine State, where many of the Rohingya Muslim minority resided.

After fighters from the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (Arsa) launched deadly attacks on more than 30 police posts there, Myanmar troops, backed by local Buddhist mobs, launched a wave of violence, prompting a mass exodus of Rohingya.

Refugees recounted entire villages being burned down and the mass killing of civilians, while numerous survivors and eyewitnesses provided testimony that the Myanmar military had also raped and abused Rohingya women and girls.

The ICJ determined that around 10,000 Rohingya were "violently killed" during the clearance operation, while more than 700,000 are thought to have fled to Bangladesh by foot or by sea. The court found that approximately 815,000 had been targeted in some way.

Iwasawa said Myanmar's military engaged in "indiscriminate" killings, the execution of men, "widespread" sexual violence, "extreme violence" against children and the deliberate burning of Rohingya homes.

He said the military had also attacked Rohingya as they were fleeing to Bangladesh.

Myanmar, he added, had engaged in "extensive destruction of evidence" by burning or disposing of bodies, burned and bulldozed sites that were cleared and failed to prosecute those who had perpetrated the acts of violence.

Image source, Getty Images

Image caption,

Rohingyas at the Cox's Bazar camp in Bangladesh, where around a million refugees now reside, watched the verdict live

While the ICJ recognised the role Arsa played, it found there was "overlap" between an "anti-Rohingya hate speech campaign" - which portrayed the Rohingya as "sub-human" and "a violent threat" - and the clearance operations that made violence against the population more likely.

Myanmar consistently denied genocide against the Rohingya, saying its operations had targeted militant or insurgent threats in response to the Arsa attacks.

In January, government representative Ko Ko Hlaing told the ICJ that the country "was not obliged to remain idle and allow terrorists to have free reign". He said he had "no comment" following Thursday's verdict.

The ICJ also looked at the wider treatment of Rohingya leading up to the clearance operation and found that policies like limiting married couples to two children were discriminatory and aimed to erode their rights.

It said Myanmar had an obligation to pay proportionate reparations, but said an exact figure could be determined at a later date.

Image source, Getty Images

Image caption,

ICJ president Yuji Iwasawa said Myanmar had the "intention to destroy" a substantial part of the Rohingya population

'Recognition of our suffering'

The court's decision was welcomed by Rohingya communities and human rights groups.

"This is like formal recognition of our suffering," says Mohammed Nowkim, a Rohingya who was driven out of Rakhine in 2017 and now lives in Canada. "The Rohingya have been waiting for justice for decades."

Human Rights Watch said the ruling was "long-awaited recognition of the suffering the Rohingya have endured".

Meanwhile, UN human rights chief Volker Türk said the "suffering, misery and humiliation" inflicted on the Rohingya people was a "stain on the conscience of humanity". He added that the court's decision "must now translate into real action".

To implicate the Myanmar government in genocide, the court had to determine not just that terrible acts had been committed, but that there was an intent on the part of officials or arms of the state to partially or completely destroy the group.

Thursday's ruling is without precedent. Myanmar now carries the stain of being the first state to have been found to have violated the 1948 Genocide Convention.

The ICJ has only twice before ruled on claims of state-backed genocide in the years since the Genocide Convention was signed in the aftermath of the Holocaust, in both cases finding there was insufficient evidence to attribute the actions to the state.

Dozens of individuals have been found guilty of genocide, but finding their actions were at the direct behest of the state requires a higher evidential bar to prove genocide, the gravest of crimes under international law.

Philippe Sands KC, a top human rights lawyer who helped bring the case, described it as an "historic judgment".

He told BBC Radio 4's World at One programme that it was "right up there with the great moments of international justice: Nuremberg, Pinochet, and others", referring to the trials of Nazi leaders following World War Two and that of the Chilean dictator, respectively.

However, the ICJ is not a criminal court and its powers of enforcement are limited. It cannot send military officials to prison, while it relies on the UN Security Council and political pressure to impose its rulings.

The ruling will, though, have implications for other genocide cases pending with the ICJ, including one brought by South Africa against Israel over its war in Gaza.

Antonia Mulvey, executive director of Legal Action Worldwide, told the BBC that the court had not accepted Myanmar's counter-terrorism defence and had found for the first time that rape and sexual violence was an act of genocide, positions it would bear in mind for future cases.

Following Thursday's ruling, UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the government was ordering Myanmar's defence attaché be expelled and that he was summoning its charge d'affaires.

He pledged to set out "further action in the coming days to ensure those responsible are held to account" after a cross-party group of MPs called for the government to resume sanctions against Myanmar's military.

translation.summary: 国际法院这项前所未有的裁决，涉及2017年造成数千人死亡的军事镇压。
translation.label: 机器翻译

blocks.text: 图表说明，
视频：种族灭绝判决对罗兴亚社区将“意义重大”
亚历克·菲利普斯、安娜·霍利根发自海牙报道，以及东南亚记者乔纳森·黑德
国际法院（ICJ）裁定缅甸对其罗兴亚少数群体犯下种族灭绝罪。
该判决标志着国际法院首次认定一个国家犯下种族灭绝罪行。
联合国最高司法机构院长岩泽雄司表示，缅甸有“毁灭意图”，旨在消灭罗兴亚人口中的相当一部分，并“大规模销毁证据”以掩盖罪行。
2017年的军事镇压造成数千名罗兴亚人死亡，并迫使逾70万人逃离以佛教徒为主的缅甸（旧称 Burma）。缅甸否认对其提出的指控，称其部队是在回应武装团体的袭击。
法院周四认定，“根据已掌握的证据，种族灭绝意图是唯一合理的推断”。
该判决由一组来自世界各地的法官以九票对六票的多数作出。国际法院还以多数认定，缅甸违反了《1948年种族灭绝公约》的其他若干条款。
冈比亚提起的这起案件，核心是2017年在若开邦发起的所谓“清剿行动”，当时许多罗兴亚穆斯林少数群体居住在那里。
若开罗兴亚救世军（Arsa）武装人员对当地30多个警察哨所发动致命袭击后，缅甸军队在当地佛教徒暴徒的支持下掀起一轮暴力，促使罗兴亚人大规模逃离。
难民们讲述了整座村庄被烧毁、平民遭到大规模杀害的情形，许多幸存者和目击者还作证称，缅甸军方也强奸并虐待了罗兴亚妇女和女童。
国际法院认定，约1万名罗兴亚人在清剿行动中被“暴力杀害”，另有逾70万人据信徒步或乘船逃往孟加拉国。法院认定，约81.5万人以某种方式成为打击目标。
岩泽雄司表示，缅甸军方实施了“无差别”杀戮、处决男性、“大规模”性暴力、针对儿童的“极端暴力”，并蓄意焚烧罗兴亚人的房屋。
他说，军方还曾在罗兴亚人逃往孟加拉国途中对他们发动攻击。
他补充说，缅甸“大规模销毁证据”，焚烧或处置尸体，焚毁并用推土机铲平已被清剿的地点，而且未能起诉实施这些暴力行为的人。

blocks.alt: Rohingya refugees watch the International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruling over whether Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya Muslims, on a screen at a camp in Bangladesh's Cox's Bazar

blocks.text: 图片来源：Getty Images
图片说明，
在孟加拉国科克斯巴扎难民营（目前约有一百万难民居住于此），罗兴亚人观看了判决直播
国际法院虽然承认 Arsa 所扮演的角色，但认定一场将罗兴亚人描绘成“低等人”和“暴力威胁”的“反罗兴亚仇恨言论运动”，与清剿行动之间存在“重叠”，从而使针对该群体的暴力更可能发生。
缅甸一直否认对罗兴亚人实施种族灭绝，称其行动是针对武装分子或叛乱威胁，以回应 Arsa 的袭击。
今年1月，政府代表哥哥伦在国际法院表示，该国“没有义务袖手旁观，任由恐怖分子为所欲为”。周四裁决后，他说自己“不予置评”。
国际法院还审视了清剿行动之前对罗兴亚人的更广泛待遇，认定诸如限制已婚夫妇只能生育两个孩子等政策具有歧视性，意在削弱他们的权利。
法院称，缅甸有义务支付相称的赔偿，但具体金额可在日后确定。

blocks.alt: International Court of Justice (ICJ) President Iwasawa Yuji presides over the verdict, wearing a judge's cloak.

blocks.text: 图片来源：Getty Images
图片说明，
国际法院院长岩泽雄司表示，缅甸有“毁灭意图”，旨在消灭罗兴亚人口中的相当一部分
“对我们所受迫害的承认”
法院的裁决受到罗兴亚社区和人权组织的欢迎。
“这像是对我们所受迫害的正式承认，”2017年被赶出若开、现居加拿大的罗兴亚人穆罕默德·诺金说。“罗兴亚人等待正义已经数十年。”
人权观察称，该裁决是“对罗兴亚人所受迫害期待已久的承认”。
与此同时，联合国人权事务高级专员福尔克尔·蒂尔克表示，强加给罗兴亚人的“苦难、痛苦和屈辱”是“人类良知上的污点”。他补充说，法院的裁决“现在必须转化为实际行动”。
要将缅甸政府牵入种族灭绝罪，法院不仅必须认定发生了残暴行为，还必须认定官员或国家机构有部分或全部消灭该群体的意图。
周四的裁决史无前例。缅甸从此背上了作为第一个被认定违反《1948年种族灭绝公约》的国家这一污名。
自大屠杀之后《种族灭绝公约》签署以来，国际法院此前仅两次就由国家主导的种族灭绝指控作出裁决，两次都认定没有足够证据将相关行为归因于国家。
已有数十人被认定犯有种族灭绝罪，但要认定他们的行为是直接受国家指使，从而证明这一国际法上最严重的罪行，所需的证据门槛更高。
协助提起此案的顶尖人权律师 Philippe Sands KC 称之为“历史性判决”。
他在 BBC Radio 4 的 World at One 节目中表示，这“足以跻身国际正义的伟大时刻之列：纽伦堡、皮诺切特以及其他”，分别指的是二战后对纳粹领导人的审判和对智利独裁者的审判。
不过，国际法院不是刑事法院，其执行权有限。它不能将军方官员投入监狱，其裁决的落实有赖于联合国安理会和政治压力。
不过，该裁决也会对国际法院审理中的其他种族灭绝案件产生影响，包括南非就加沙战争对以色列提起的案件。
Legal Action Worldwide 执行董事安东尼娅·马尔维对 BBC 表示，法院没有接受缅甸的反恐辩护，并首次认定强奸和性暴力属于种族灭绝行为，这些立场将在今后的案件中被纳入考量。
周四裁决后，英国外交大臣埃德·米利班德表示，政府已下令驱逐缅甸国防武官，并且他将召见缅甸临时代办。
在一个跨党派议员团体呼吁政府恢复对缅甸军方的制裁后，他承诺将“在未来几天内提出进一步行动，确保责任人受到追究”。

items.title: Susan Smith denied parole again 32 years after drowning her two sons
items.summary: This is the second time Smith has requested to be released from prison for killing the two boys, who were both under the age of four at the time.
items.body:
Image source, Getty Images

Image caption,

Smith was convicted of killing her two sons in 1994

A South Carolina woman who admitted to drowning her two sons 32 years ago is requesting, for a second time, to be released on parole.

Susan Smith, 55, was convicted of killing her boys by strapping them into their car seats and letting her vehicle roll into a lake in 1994.

items.summary: EHRC chair says ‘misinformation’ about guidance issued after supreme court ruling has created ‘more anxiety’ The head of the UK’s equalities watchdog has urged people to “take the temperature down” on reaction to guidance issued on single-sex spaces. Mary-Ann Stephenson, the chair of the Equality an…
items.body:
Mary-Ann Stephenson made the comments during a session of the Scottish parliament’s equalities, human rights and civil justice committee. Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PA

Mary-Ann Stephenson made the comments during a session of the Scottish parliament’s equalities, human rights and civil justice committee. Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PA

‘Take temperature down’ over guidance on single-sex spaces, head of UK equalities body urges

EHRC chair says ‘misinformation’ about guidance issued after supreme court ruling has created ‘more anxiety’

The head of the UK’s equalities watchdog has urged people to “take the temperature down” on reaction to guidance issued on single-sex spaces.

Mary-Ann Stephenson, the chair of the Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC), appearing before MSPs in Holyrood, said “misinformation” over the body’s guidance had created “more anxiety among people”.

The guidance was released earlier this year after a ruling by the supreme court that sex in the Equality Act 2010 referred to biological sex.

The ruling has caused concern among transgender people in Scotland, according to organisations who also appeared before the Scottish parliament’s equalities, human rights and civil justice committee on Thursday, with some choosing not to seek medical attention as a result.

Stephenson told the committee: “It is really clear that there are significant numbers of trans people, including, particularly, maybe younger trans people, who feel very, very anxious at the moment and I think that some of that is to do with the fact that what they thought the law entitled them to, it turned out wasn’t the case.”

She added: “I think that some of this is about the way in which the code has been characterised and talked about in really inflated language. Saying that it excludes all trans people from public life, that there’s going to be genital checks to ensure people’s access to services.

“I can understand feelings are high, people are upset, but actually, it doesn’t help.

“What it does is create more anxiety among people about things that actually the law doesn’t say, the code doesn’t say, and I think it’s incumbent on all of us to try to take the temperature down a little bit in this area and to try to recognise that at the heart of the Equality Act is trying to build a society where everybody is able to live with dignity and have access to the services they need, not to face discrimination.”

The guidance has had an effect on various areas of life for transgender people, according to organisations who support them, including access to leisure facilities and healthcare settings.

Florence Oulds, the policy and public affairs coordinator at the charity Scottish Trans, told of cases in which people had refused to go to hospital.

‘Progress takes time’: Stonewall CEO on turning down the heat on the trans debate

Read more

“We are aware of at least three trans people we’ve spoken to and other trans people we’ve heard evidence from who have not gone to hospital against medical advice because they are concerned about where they’ll be placed on a ward,” she told MSPs. “I think that’s a very common sentiment.”

Oulds also claimed the guidance lacked clarity, saying the code of practice was “just fundamentally a very confusing and difficult document to follow”.

Oulds said the EHCR “often instructs organisations to seek legal advice but there does seem to be an unbelievably wide range of legal advice in this area, often completely conflicting”.

“I have heard from organisations who are trans-inclusive, want to do the right thing, want to see if they can remain trans-inclusive while still remaining in the law, who have spent lots of money on legal advice and not really got anywhere.”

Stephenson said she “would disagree with that interpretation” and added: “I think the code is actually quite straightforward.”

items.title: Southern California braced for fierce storm after record rain in San Francisco
items.summary: Planes temporarily grounded, roads flooded and tens of thousands lose power, with evacuations in south of state Southern California braced for the arrival of a fierce winter storm that already set records for rainfall in the north of the state. Los Angeles authorities urged residents in the Palisade…
items.body:
Crews work at the flooded area on Alemany Blvd at the entrance of Highway 101 during heavy rain in San Francisco, California, on Wednesday. Photograph: Tayfun Coşkun/Anadolu/Getty Images

Crews work at the flooded area on Alemany Blvd at the entrance of Highway 101 during heavy rain in San Francisco, California, on Wednesday. Photograph: Tayfun Coşkun/Anadolu/Getty Images

San Francisco breaks rain record as atmospheric river buffets California

Planes temporarily grounded, roads flooded and tens of thousands lose power, with evacuations in south of state

Heavy rain and high winds battered the US west coast, temporarily grounding planes at San Francisco’s airport, flooding roads in Napa county and forcing evacuations in southern California.

Record-breaking rain lashes California’s Bay area as ‘atmospheric river’ arrives

Read more

The fierce storm, called an atmospheric river, moved from north to south across the state. On Wednesday, San Francisco broke a rain record previously set in 1917. The city’s fire department responded to hundreds of calls, many of which related to flooding, along with downed trees and electrical wires. Flights at San Francisco airport were delayed hours because of wind.

Areas along the city’s Embarcadero were flooded as waves crashed over barricades recently installed to prevent flooding near the Ferry Building, a waterfront landmark. Officials canceled several ferries leading from the city due to the storm.

Tens of thousands of households lost power across the region.

Several highways were blocked by flooding or debris in nearby Napa, Marin, San Mateo and Santa Clara counties. South of San Francisco, a 47-mile (76km) segment of Highway 1 near Big Sur was closed on Wednesday for similar reasons.

california precipitation chart

In southern California, authorities issued evacuation orders as the storm moved south. The Los Angeles county fire department urged residents in the Palisades, Hurst and Sunset burn scar areas to leave, warning of a risk of debris flows.

And in the mountains, heavy snows forced the closure of highways in the Tahoe area. Snow accumulations of up to 4ft (1.2 meters) were forecast through Friday in the highest portions of the Sierra Nevada.

Atmospheric rivers, huge currents of water vapor that can carry as much or even more water than an actual river, have been growing stronger and deadlier in recent years. In the relatively dry western US, atmospheric river storms provide both essential precipitation and flood risk.

A car rests in floodwater near the 101 freeway on Wednesday in Sausalito, California. Photograph: Benjamin Fanjoy/Getty Images

The Golden state is bracing for more weather challenges in the week ahead, when fresh rain is set to coincide with high tides.

items.title: ‘Everyone struggled for this justice’: tears in court as Rohingya vindicated in Myanmar genocide ruling
items.summary: Relief in the immediate aftermath of a landmark ruling, but what happens next is in the hands of governments around the world There were tears in the halls of The Hague in the Netherlands and an eruption of applause in the refugee camps of Bangladesh as the scattered communities of Rohingya watched…
items.body:
Rohingya refugees at their camp in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh, react during a live broadcast of the international court of justice Myanmar genocide ruling. Photograph: Yassin Abdumonab/EPA

Rohingya refugees at their camp in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh, react during a live broadcast of the international court of justice Myanmar genocide ruling. Photograph: Yassin Abdumonab/EPA

‘Everyone struggled for this justice’: tears in court as Rohingya vindicated in Myanmar genocide ruling

Relief in the immediate aftermath of a landmark ruling, but what happens next is in the hands of governments around the world

There were tears in the halls of The Hague in the Netherlands and an eruption of applause in the refugee camps of Bangladesh as the scattered communities of Rohingya watched the UN’s top court rule the Myanmar military had committed genocide against them.

For almost a decade, the Rohingya have awaited this moment; recognition from the international court of justice (ICJ) that Myanmar in 2017 intentionally tried to destroy the mostly Muslim minority group through a campaign of mass killings and rape. More than 10,000 Rohingya were killed and 700,000 fled to neighbouring Bangladesh.

By the time they spilled into the court’s halls, the relief was evident. A Rohingya community leader threw a big thumbs up as he left the courtroom and others immediately took out their phones to call family in the refugee camps.

Salma, 30, a Rohingya survivor who lost family members in the 2017 genocide, said: “Everyone worked hard and struggled for this justice, for this cause. When they hear it today, everyone will be happy, thank God. I don’t know how to express it or even what to do with myself.”

The Gambian justice minister Dawda Jallow, centre, speaking at the ICJ in The Hague on Thursday: ‘The victory belongs to the Rohingya. They survived. They testified. And today, they will believe.’ Photograph: Jeroen Jumelet/ANP/AFP/Getty Images

Another Rohingya present, who cannot be named because of safety concerns, said they cried as the judge went through each of the rulings.

“During the last few minutes I couldn’t even sit down any more, I had to move to the back because I didn’t know how I’d react,” they said. “I saw some of the other Rohingya around me crying. They were so emotional.

“Now the responsibility is with the international governments. It has been declared genocide now and they have to act.”

In Bangladesh, where most of the Rohingya population have lived – in the world’s largest refugee camp – since being forced to flee in 2017, the verdict was translated into the Rohingya language for the crowds who had gathered to watch on screens specially set up for the purpose.

They immediately leapt up, cheering, applauding and shouting gratitude for the Gambia – the faraway African nation that brought the case to the ICJ on behalf of the stateless minority. Many held posters that read “Thank You Gambia” and “Justice = Safe Return”.

“Since we arrived here, we have been waiting and looking forward to this justice,” said Farida Khatun, 50, who has been a refugee in Bangladesh since 2017, when her village, Tula Toli, was targeted by soldiers. The village in north-western Myanmar, near the Bangladesh border, was the scene of a massacre in August of that year, with reports of mass killings and gang rapes.

She said, however, that she does not expect to be able to return home. Tula Toli was completely destroyed by Myanmar’s forces and no longer exists. “Even though today’s verdict makes us happy, my heart still cannot believe that they will take us back in true peace.”

The case has taken seven years to reach this point, with Rohingya researchers working to collect testimony from survivors. The initial hope for justice had faded during the long wait for a ruling. Many were also left deflated during early hearings when the one-time pro-democracy hero Aung San Suu Kyi defended the Myanmar military at The Hague.

Yusuf Ali, a Rohingya justice campaigner, outside the ICJ in The Hague on the day of the ruling. Photograph: Kaamil Ahmed/The Guardian

Before today’s ruling, some were optimistic, others were prepared to be disappointed, but all said they knew themselves that they were victims of genocide.

The tension was finally released when the court declared Myanmar was responsible for genocide against the Rohingya, highlighting the use of sexual violence and attacks on children alongside the killing of Rohingya who tried to flee violence, which it said meant the violence amounted to more than ethnic cleansing.

The court ordered Myanmar to provide reparations for the Rohingya and end continuing breaches of the genocide convention.

Rohingya refugees in Cox’s Bazar thank the Gambia for its role as they watch a live broadcast of the ICJ Myanmar genocide ruling. Photograph: Yassin Abdumonab/EPA

There is now also an international criminal court investigation into the violence of 2017, looking specifically at the crime of mass deportation, and for which prosecutors in 2024 sought an arrest warrant for Myanmar’s leader, Min Aung Hlaing.

With continuing violence against the Rohingya, the possibility of a return to Myanmar, as happened after previous exoduses to Bangladesh in 1978 and the early 1990s, remains unlikely.

But many hope the ICJ ruling will be the start of a process of ensuring justice and lead to real international pressure to ensure their safety in Myanmar.

“We will be able to return to our homeland – with our rights, with our citizenship, and having received our full security. We will be able to return,” says Salma.

Prosecutors allege British woman ‘trying to find someone who would kill her’ lured to US and murdered

Sonia Exelby’s disappearance sparked an international search. The accused man, Dwain Hall, denies murdering her

Prosecutors in Ocala, Florida, have been laying out an extraordinary criminal case against Dwain C Hall, an auto repair and tow truck driver accused of kidnapping and murdering Sonia Exelby, of Portsmouth, England.

Prosecutors allege that Hall lured Exelby to the US before killing her in October last year and burying her body in a shallow grave in Marion Oaks. Hall has pleaded not guilty to the charges.

Exelby’s disappearance from her home sparked an international investigation. Prosecutors this week described how she suffered from mental illness. After Hall’s arrest in November 2025, investigators said that Exelby had traveled to Florida after posting online about wanting someone to end her life.

Hall’s arrest affidavit said that Exelby had previously expressed suicidal thoughts and investigators alleged that Hall knew about her struggles and used that vulnerability to bring her to Florida, the Ocala Starbanner reported.

The authorities have said Exelby boarded a flight to the US seemingly with an intention “to be possibly sexually abused, tortured, and murdered by unknown individuals living in the United States”.

After Exelby traveled to the US in October 2025, authorities say Hall picked her up from Gainesville airport in central Florida. He drove her to an Airbnb rental, where investigators later found evidence they say connected him to her disappearance and death, including transactions on her bank cards and a video of Exelby on Hall’s cellphone.

An undated handout photo of Dwain Hall issued by the Florida department of law enforcement. Photograph: Florida department of law enforcement/PA

In a text message from Exelby’s phone to a friend, she said she felt scared and trapped, according to the arrest affidavit. “I’m sorry, he keeps taking my phone, he doesn’t trust me with it,” she wrote. “He made it clear there was no way out unless I shoot him.”

In opening statements this week, assistant state attorney Amy Berndt said Exelby’s parents struggled with mental illness and addiction and that their daughter had also struggled with mental illness and twice attempted suicide.

She had visited a website depicting graphic sexual abuse of women, where Hall was among several men who contacted her.

Berndt said in court that Exelby “was trying to find some substitute” to the self-harm. “Unfortunately, she found another outlet.” Berndt said Exelby was “trying to find someone who would kill her”.

“Unfortunately there was no shortage of depraved men willing to kill Sonia in the most torturous and vile ways possible,” Berndt added.

After she disappeared from her home, a former boyfriend, Stevie Hunt, contacted the authorities, the court heard.

In court, Hunt described Exelby as a kind, beautiful and loving woman, while her sister talked about their difficult childhood. Hunt told the court that Exelby experienced mood swings that sometimes lasted for days and had been in therapy for more than a decade.

Hall has denied killing Exelby but acknowledged in a police interview that he had been in contact with her and that the two had been intimate. Evidence linking Hall to Exelby’s death includes a shovel with Exelby’s blood on it, cellphone data, and a knife recovered from a friend of the defendant.

Prosecutors have said jurors will be shown photographs and surveillance video of Hall making purchases including rope, a shovel, deodorant and other items at a local Walmart store.

Hall’s defense attorney Junior Barrett said in opening statements that his client was not a murderer and asked jurors to carefully consider the facts, witness testimony and circumstances of the case.

“We believe that when you listen to all the facts and evidence in this case, you will arrive at the decision that Dwain Hall did not murder,” Barrett said.

The case continues.

Four UK men convicted of sexual assault and rape of woman at invitation of husband

Former Tory councillor advertised ex-wife on swinging websites and drugged and bound her for sex

Four men have been convicted of sexually assaulting and raping a woman at the invitation of her husband who had drugged and bound her.

Philip Young, 50, advertised his then wife, Joanne Young, on dating and swinging websites, presenting it as a “kink” for both of them, Winchester crown court heard. In fact, he had been sedating her, plunging her into an “inanimate state” where anything could be done to her by whoever answered the adverts, jurors were told.

The former Conservative councillor pleaded guilty earlier in the year to dozens of charges of abuse against his former wife, who has waived her right to anonymity.

Connor Sanderson-Doyle, 32; Richard Wilkins, 62; Norman Macksoni, 48; and Mohammed Hassan, 38, were convicted of various offences against Joanne Young after a three-week trial.

Sanderson-Doyle, a Ministry of Defence contractor from Swindon, was convicted of sexual assault and assault by penetration; Wilkins, a taxi driver from Swindon, was found guilty of assault by penetration and rape; Macksoni, a former DJ and waste management worker from Bedfordshire, was convicted of rape; and Hassan, also from Swindon, was found guilty of sexual assault.

A further defendant, Dean Hamilton, 47, from Somerset, has admitted one charge of assault by penetration, two of sexual assault and one of rape.

The case has drawn comparisons to that of Gisèle Pelicot, who was drugged by her husband and raped by dozens of strangers in France. It can now be revealed that Wiltshire police received advice from the Pelicot investigators on how to approach their inquiries.

The men, including Young, will be sentenced together at a later date.

items.body:
Young pleaded guilty to 50 offences including drugging, raping and sexually assaulting Joanne, who has been praised for her bravery. Composite: Guardian Design/PA

Young pleaded guilty to 50 offences including drugging, raping and sexually assaulting Joanne, who has been praised for her bravery. Composite: Guardian Design/PA

Spiked nightcaps and invitations to strangers: how Philip Young sexually abused his wife for 15 years

Joanne Young, who has waived anonymity, was subjected to years of drugging and rape by former Swindon councillor, who invited other men to assault her

When Philip Young served as a Conservative party councillor for Swindon council, his contemporaries viewed him as a perfectly normal family man with “no edge to him”.

But behind closed doors he orchestrated a systematic campaign of abuse against his then wife, Joanne Young, secretly administering sedatives to render her unconscious, disoriented and amnesiac. Over a period of at least 15 years, he and other men raped and sexually assaulted her in her own bed at their home in Swindon.

The father of three pleaded guilty to more than 50 offences, including drugging, raping and sexually assaulting Joanne, who has been praised for her bravery in waiving her anonymity. His co-accused Connor Sanderson-Doyle, Richard Wilkins, Norman Macksoni and Mohammed Hassan were convicted by a jury of their involvement. Another man, Dean Hamilton, pleaded guilty in February to rape.

The high-profile case has drawn comparisons to the Gisèle Pelicot trial in France, and it can now be revealed that the Crown Prosecution Service and Wiltshire police met the French team of investigators and prosecutors for advice.

A mural reading ‘Gisele, women thank you’ in Avignon, southern France. Photograph: Christophe Simon/AFP/Getty Images

Testimony and police interviews paint a picture of a carefully maintained domestic facade masking a predatory reality. Joanne, who was married to Young for 20 years and had been with him since 2002, described their relationship as traditionally monogamous and her own preferences as strictly “vanilla”.

Because of his heavy snoring, they slept in separate rooms, with Joanne eventually occupying a spacious second-floor loft conversion featuring a large black headboard and purple bedding.

Unknown to her, Young was exploiting this arrangement, and taking advantage of a common evening routine – sharing a nightcap of vodka after returning from social occasions – to spike her drinks with sedatives including zolpidem and ketamine that he is now believed to have bought online from countries including India.

The nightmare began to unravel on the night of 18 February 2023 after an evening out at the Blunsdon Arms. Joanne half-woke to find herself wearing a soft blindfold and wrist restraints, with a stranger’s hand on her wrist. She realised an unknown man was in her bedroom. When she attempted to move, Young whispered “get down”, causing the intruder to duck. Severely shortsighted and without her glasses, Joanne fled to the en suite bathroom and locked herself inside.

The following morning, Young apologised, claiming he had invited a man over from an online forum just to watch. The confession left Joanne deeply traumatised and questioning her marriage. She struggled to access counselling, while also managing impending redundancies at their shared business, a consulting firm.

The full scale of Young’s twisted operation was exposed after the National Crime Agency flagged illegal activity linked to him – the uploading of a bestiality image – on the messaging and livestreaming app Kik. Wiltshire police raided his home in July 2024.

Court artist sketch of Philip Young (right) appearing at Swindon magistrates court. Photograph: Elizabeth Cook/PA

Officers discovered digital caches of videos showing his then wife incapacitated, restrained and being sexually assaulted by a range of strangers, who it later emerged had been recruited via Craigslist, Grindr, Reddit and swinging websites. Young used multiple online aliases – such as “londonmonkey” – and posted advertisements across major cities such as London, Bristol and Bath, often messaging under the guise of Joanne.

He used at least 20 unique advertisement IDs and the titles included “Fuck my tied and blindfolded wife – mw4m – 35 (North Swindon)” and “Fuck my wife – 18th September – Central Bath hotel – mw4m”. The abbreviation “mw4m” was used in the posts to denote a man and woman looking for a man.

In a police interview on 4 July 2024, Young openly discussed his sexual fantasies, describing himself as “monogamous” – he had no interest in sleeping with other women – but saying he enjoyed “wife sharing”, or seeing his wife have sex with other men. He admitted to sharing images exclusively of his wife and claimed her interest in involving third parties varied, adding that “she changes at times”.

He told officers that in intimate moments his wife would sometimes tell him to “do what you want” and he would use Grindr to find men nearby to quickly arrive and “strip and join in”. He said his wife would usually be in bed, “blindfolded and tied” by her arms to the bed head, acting “submissive” while engaging with other men.

But Joanne later told detectives and the court she did not consent to other men having sex with her, adding the relationship “was monogamous, always monogamous”.

The following day, 5 July 2024, Young answered “no comment” to all questions put to him by officers. Hair sample analysis conducted by a forensic toxicologist who also worked on the Pelicot trial revealed traces of ketamine and zolpidem in Joanne’s hair. Residues of zolpidem were also detected inside a plastic bag found in Young’s old bedside table.

In January, Young pleaded guilty at Winchester crown court to 11 counts of rape and 11 counts of administering a substance with intent to stupefy Joanne. He also admitted 14 counts of voyeurism, including a single count that covered at least 200 acts of voyeurism; seven counts of assault by penetration; four counts of sexual assault and one count of publishing obscene articles on at least 500 occasions. He later admitted to charges of making indecent images of children, one count of possessing a prohibited image of a child, and four charges of possessing an extreme pornographic image.

But four of his co-accused denied charges of rape and sexual assault, which meant Joanne was subjected to the brutal process of a trial, in which she was again praised for giving evidence to the court. The jury rejected the defendants’ claims that they believed the acts were consensual, securing guilty verdicts across all counts for the co-accused.

Still from police body-worn video showing the arrest of Connor Sanderson-Doyle. Photograph: Wiltshire Police/PA

Sanderson-Doyle, a Ministry of Defence contractor recruited via Craigslist in 2016 and captured on video assaulting the victim while wearing a balaclava, was convicted of sexual assault and assault by penetration.

Wilkins, a 62-year-old taxi driver who participated in July 2016, recorded performing a sex act on the sleeping and snoring victim, was found guilty of assault by penetration and rape.

Macksoni, a waste management worker who communicated with Young using the codename “Blunsdon” and was filmed abusing Joanne in February 2017, was convicted of rape.

Hassan, who was involved in the February 2023 incident in which Joanne woke up and discovered a stranger in her room, was found guilty of sexual assault.

A court artist sketch of (left to right) Macksoni, Sanderson-Doyle, Wilkins, Hassan and Hamilton at Swindon magistrates court in December 2025. Photograph: Elizabeth Cook/PA

Friends who socialised with the couple – sharing meals at the Blunsdon Arms and Greek restaurants, and playing Trivial Pursuit – recalled an outwardly normal family life with three children.

However, friends such as Andrew and Emma Brown and Rachel Williams said they had frequently noticed Young glued to his mobile phone during gatherings, an obsession now recognised as coordinating with strangers online.

It emerged in the trial that a potential opportunity to catch Young 10 years earlier may have been missed. In 2015, officers investigated an impounded package from India addressed to Young containing 120 zolpidem tablets – a class C drug known as a potential “date rape” substance. Young claimed ignorance, suggesting someone had misused his business details. An intelligence report was filed but no further action was taken.

A spokesperson for Wiltshire police said it was “understandable that questions may be asked” with the benefit of hindsight. “However, based on the information available at the time, the attending officer’s actions were both appropriate and proportionate,” they added.

“At that point, Young was a person of previously good character, with no criminal convictions, and there was no intelligence, information or evidence to suggest he posed a risk of committing the serious offences that have since come to light. The interaction was dealt with reasonably and in line with the information known at the time.”

Young later obtained multiple legitimate prescriptions for zolpidem and zopiclone from his GP between 2018 and 2022.

The revelations have sent shock waves through political circles in Swindon. A senior non-elected official close to Swindon borough council when Young served expressed profound shock at the former councillor’s conviction, telling the Guardian the revelations were “horrific” and “hideous”.

Young, who served as a cabinet member for regeneration and economic development between 2007 and 2010, was remembered as a progressive and engaging colleague. He held the political lead for Forward Swindon, an urban regeneration company responsible for revamping the town’s railway station forecourt among other projects, and liaised with the local business improvement district.

According to the source, the council was a difficult authority with challenging members at the time, but Young stood out as a clear exception. “He was one of the much more easy-to-get-along-with members [and] seemed to be considerate of staff,” the official noted, describing his approach as representing the “more modern thinking of councillors”.

The official said Young had shown no warning signs of his future criminal behaviour, in either his language or demeanour. “There was absolutely … no reason given to think that there was something unusual about this fellow,” the official said, adding that colleagues had generally considered Young to be “one of the good guys”.

A Conservative party source, who was close to the council at the time Young served, told the Guardian of the anger and betrayal they had felt upon learning of the former councillor’s crimes, saying the revelations had come as a “complete shock”.

Young was viewed as a highly capable and “brilliant councillor” who played a hands-on role in trying to revive Swindon’s town centre after the financial crash, they said. They revealed that Young had been so highly regarded for his public speaking and specialised skills that he was actively encouraged to run for council leader before he stepped down to become a director at the New Swindon Company.

Publicly, Young presented as a “perfectly normal family man” and successful business owner with “no edge to him”. “He wasn’t creepy in any way … I would never, ever have suspected anything untoward,” the source said.

Learning of the offences from a national newspaper reporter last Christmas had left former colleagues “beyond shocked” and “speechless”, they said. Expressing sympathy for the victims and for Young’s children, regarding the legacy he had left them, the source said the scale of his deception made them wonder “if you ever know anybody”.

After the convictions, questions still remain about the extent of Young’s offending. Police later discovered a receipt for a camcorder dating back to 2011, raising investigators’ suspicions that the covert recording and abuse may have started earlier than the window covered by the charges.

Meanwhile, authorities continue efforts to identify an elusive offender captured in the digital evidence who has yet to be identified despite several police appeals. Young has been questioned via his lawyers about the identity of the individual but has not assisted with inquiries.

Friends who socialised with the couple – sharing meals at the Blunsdon Arms and Greek restaurants, and playing Trivial Pursuit – recalled an outwardly normal family life with three children.

However, friends such as Andrew and Emma Brown and Rachel Williams said they had frequently noticed Young glued to his mobile phone during gatherings, an obsession now recognised as coordinating with strangers online.

It emerged in the trial that a potential opportunity to catch Young 10 years earlier may have been missed. In 2015, officers investigated an impounded package from India addressed to Young containing 120 zolpidem tablets – a class C drug known as a potential “date rape” substance. Young claimed ignorance, suggesting someone had misused his business details. An intelligence report was filed but no further action was taken.

A spokesperson for Wiltshire police said it was “understandable that questions may be asked” with the benefit of hindsight. “However, based on the information available at the time, the attending officer’s actions were both appropriate and proportionate,” they added.

“At that point, Young was a person of previously good character, with no criminal convictions, and there was no intelligence, information or evidence to suggest he posed a risk of committing the serious offences that have since come to light. The interaction was dealt with reasonably and in line with the information known at the time.”
Young later obtained multiple legitimate prescriptions for zolpidem and zopiclone from his GP between 2018 and 2022.

The revelations have sent shock waves through political circles in Swindon. A senior non-elected official close to Swindon borough council when Young served expressed profound shock at the former councillor’s conviction, telling the Guardian the revelations were “horrific” and “hideous”.

Young, who served as a cabinet member for regeneration and economic development between 2007 and 2010, was remembered as a progressive and engaging colleague. He held the political lead for Forward Swindon, an urban regeneration company responsible for revamping the town’s railway station forecourt among other projects, and liaised with the local business improvement district.

According to the source, the council was a difficult authority with challenging members at the time, but Young stood out as a clear exception. “He was one of the much more easy-to-get-along-with members [and] seemed to be considerate of staff,” the official noted, describing his approach as representing the “more modern thinking of councillors”.

The official said Young had shown no warning signs of his future criminal behaviour, in either his language or demeanour. “There was absolutely … no reason given to think that there was something unusual about this fellow,” the official said, adding that colleagues had generally considered Young to be “one of the good guys”.

A Conservative party source, who was close to the council at the time Young served, told the Guardian of the anger and betrayal they had felt upon learning of the former councillor’s crimes, saying the revelations had come as a “complete shock”.

Young was viewed as a highly capable and “brilliant councillor” who played a hands-on role in trying to revive Swindon’s town centre after the financial crash, they said. They revealed that Young had been so highly regarded for his public speaking and specialised skills that he was actively encouraged to run for council leader before he stepped down to become a director at the New Swindon Company.

Publicly, Young presented as a “perfectly normal family man” and successful business owner with “no edge to him”. “He wasn’t creepy in any way … I would never, ever have suspected anything untoward,” the source said.

Learning of the offences from a national newspaper reporter last Christmas had left former colleagues “beyond shocked” and “speechless”, they said. Expressing sympathy for the victims and for Young’s children, regarding the legacy he had left them, the source said the scale of his deception made them wonder “if you ever know anybody”.

After the convictions, questions still remain about the extent of Young’s offending. Police later discovered a receipt for a camcorder dating back to 2011, raising investigators’ suspicions that the covert recording and abuse may have started earlier than the window covered by the charges.

Meanwhile, authorities continue efforts to identify an elusive offender captured in the digital evidence who has yet to be identified despite several police appeals. Young has been questioned via his lawyers about the identity of the individual but has not assisted with inquiries.

items.summary: Jamie Davis falls just short as Democrats across south wonder whether blue wave could have been even bigger Democrats are celebrating after, with Mary Peltola’s victory in Alaska, they have officially secured 56 Senate seats after the midterm elections. But Jamie Davis, who lost an incredibly close…
items.body:
Jamie Davis on election night in Baton Rouge. ‘I am that moderate Democrat that comes from real rural Louisiana.’ Photograph: Kathleen Flynn/Reuters

Jamie Davis on election night in Baton Rouge. ‘I am that moderate Democrat that comes from real rural Louisiana.’ Photograph: Kathleen Flynn/Reuters

‘It stings to come close’: Louisiana Democrat’s narrow failure to make it 57 Senate seats

Jamie Davis falls just short as Democrats across south wonder whether blue wave could have been even bigger

Democrats are celebrating after, with Mary Peltola’s victory in Alaska, they have officially secured 56 Senate seats after the midterm elections. But Jamie Davis, who lost an incredibly close election for a Senate seat in Louisiana and could have made it 57, told the Guardian it “stings to come close”.

In Louisiana, which has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 2008, Davis lost to the Republican congresswoman Julia Letlow 49.1% to 50.9%. He was about 25,000 votes short in a state that cast about 1.5m votes.

“Truthfully, I mean, it kind of stings to come close, but what hurts more than anything else is the fact that, still today, people don’t realize and know what we did,” Davis said. “There are still some people out there right now today who do not realize that I only came within a point – I think it’s one point, 1.1 or 1.2 points of winning this election.”

Across the south, Democrats are now wondering what might have been, as other Senate seats were also close. Barry Moore beat Everett Wess in Alabama by nine points, which is a landslide in many states and a catastrophe compared with Donald Trump’s 30-point margin in 2024. Angie Nixon, whose progressive politics and opposition to the Israeli government looked like a mismatch with Florida’s conservative electorate, came within three points of unseating the Republican incumbent, Ashley Moody, in a special election.

In the weeks since, Democrats have questioned which of those states might have been winnable had the national party cast its light in the south. And many have zeroed in on Louisiana.

Unlike Florida, Louisiana is not an expensive media market. And Louisiana does not have the depth of partisan political identification to be overcome in a place like Alabama.

Turnout nationwide ran about three points higher in November than four years ago. In Louisiana, it ran eight points higher, in line with states facing competitive US Senate elections like Michigan and Maine.

Senator Bill Cassidy and Trump have long been at odds. Cassidy voted for his impeachment and asked him not to run in 2024. Trump targeted the Louisiana Republican in the primary, endorsing Letlow.

The Callais decision from the US supreme court originated in Louisiana and prompted the state to postpone primary elections and set off redistricting battles this year. Combined with Cassidy’s third-place finish in the primary, the motivating effect of these events on Black voters should have also set off alarm bells among Democratic fundraisers and operatives, Davis said.

“When it became open, that’s the time when Republicans and Democrats and independents all should have been on notice that there’s an open seat in the Senate,” Davis said. “And not just automatically think that the seat is going to turn to be Republican.”

Lutlow outraised and outspent Davis by almost two to one, though the total spending in the race – about $13m accounted for so far – is low by historic standards in Louisiana and nationally this cycle. Troy Jackson in Maine raised and spent about $25.2m in a state with about 1.4 million residents – or $18 for every Mainer – to unseat Susan Collins. Abdul El-Sayed spent about $5 per person in Michigan, buoyed by fierce national attention. Roy Cooper spent about $3.66 per person in a blowout race in North Carolina.

In Louisiana, Davis spent about $0.82 per person. Letlow spent $1.44.

Davis said he was hurt by a last-minute campaign ad, which used AI to depict him slowly walking toward the camera while a narrator falsely described his positions on abortion, gun rights, crime and immigration.

“I did not have enough campaign funds in my account to answer that ad,” Davis said, which he vowed regretfully never to allow that to happen again if he runs for statewide office. “I’m not saying that single-handed thing ended the election for me, but I will say not being able to answer it didn’t help me at all.

“But I also say that my dad always told me that you cannot depend on somebody to fight your fight for you. You can’t depend on somebody to plant a seed and you harvest it. If you plant the seed, you should harvest it.”

Davis was a political unknown a year ago, living on acreage between Red Gum and Ridgecrest, about 10 miles from the Mississippi River, in black dirt, row crop, river bottom country, way up north from New Orleans. Davis farms corn, soy, sorghum and cotton.

“I am that moderate Democrat that comes from real rural Louisiana,” Davis said. “That rural Louisiana part that most of the Democrats felt like, hey, they done forgot about us. We’re Democrats too. We don’t live in an urban area, but we still get up and go to work in the morning, we still farm, we still raise chickens, we still do country things like old-school Democrats used to do.”

items.title: Dozens missing after boat carrying migrants sinks off Senegal's coast
items.summary: At least four bodies have been recovered from the boat which was reportedly carrying between 50 and 100 people.
items.body:
Image source, AFP via Getty Images

Image caption,

The damaged boat washed ashore on a beach

ByBasillioh Rukanga

Updated 39 minutes ago

Senegalese authorities are continuing search operations after a boat reportedly carrying about 100 migrants capsized off the coast.

Initial reports said that one person had died, but some local media have reported that at least four bodies have been recovered. Dozens of people are still missing.

Personal belongings were found on the badly damaged boat, which washed ashore near the village of Yenne, south of Dakar. Search operations continued throughout Wednesday and were due to resume on Thursday.

This comes less than two weeks after a shipwreck off the coast of the north-western town of Thieppe killed at least 39 people, in one of Senegal's deadliest migration disasters.

Oumar Sow, a representative of the village chief, said the latest tragedy happened around 02:00 local time (02:00 GMT).

"Cries could be heard coming from the pirogue that were audible even from the beach," the AFP news agency quoted him as saying.

A survivor questioned by the police said there were about 100 people on the boat, including five women, AFP reported.

Police recovered identity documents, several mobile phones and personal belongings from the wreckage, including a school enrolment document.

At a cabinet meeting on Wednesday, President Diomaye Faye expressed concern about a renewed increase in irregular departure by migrants hoping to reach Europe.

He instructed the interior ministry to prepare a report examining the factors driving the dangerous journeys and proposing measures to tackle the problem.

Following last month's tragedy, Faye had urged Senegalese people not to risk their lives attempting the dangerous sea crossings.

Many thousands of people from West Africa have died or gone missing trying to flee conflict, authoritarian rule or poverty in recent years.

The UN's migration agency IOM said last month that it had recorded at least 454 deaths and disappearances off the West African coast this year alone.

It warned the figures were likely to be an underestimate, as many boats disappear without leaving survivors or a trace.

As it has become more difficult to reach Europe through North Africa, due to tighter controls and increased co-operation with European countries, migrants are increasingly targeting Spain's Canary Islands.

They often travel in wooden boats known as pirogues that are frequently overloaded and not suited to such long voyages across the Atlantic Ocean.

Most migrants arriving in the Canary Islands this year are from Senegal, according to the UN.

They are driven to leave home by limited employment opportunities, family pressures and established migration networks, according to the IOM.

On 7 November, El Hierro, one of the Canary Islands, declared a state of emergency following a surge in migrant arrivals.

It said more than 3,300 people had reached the island in about 30 boats since the beginning of the month. This amounts to almost a third of the island's population.

items.title: China, Russia and US agree peace declaration with no mention of Ukraine and Iran wars
items.summary: Xi, Putin and Trump outline priorities that include UN reform, boosting oil supplies and ‘protection of diplomatic immunity’ China, Russia and the US say they have agreed a peace statement after an unprecedented trilateral summit, but the declaration made no mention of the wars in Ukraine and Iran c…
items.body:
Press conference following the end of Apec summit – watch live

China, Russia and US agree peace declaration with no mention of Ukraine and Iran wars

Xi, Putin and Trump outline priorities that include UN reform, boosting oil supplies and ‘protection of diplomatic immunity’

• Apec summit – latest updates

China, Russia and the US have said they have agreed a peace statement after an unprecedented trilateral summit, but the declaration made no mention of the wars in Ukraine and Iran triggered by two of the participants.

The declaration on Thursday also outlined a set of priorities that included changing the UN, boosting oil supplies and what it said was the protection of diplomatic immunity.

The statement affirmed that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must not be fought”, but stopped short of suggesting the beginnings of a framework for denuclearisation.

The meeting between Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump has dominated the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit this week, with China, the host, promising it would be “groundbreaking”.

Vladimir Putin shakes hands with Donald Trump in front of the other world leaders at the Apec summit in Shenzhen, China. Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAP

“We are really making history,” Trump told Xi and Putin at the start of the meeting. “No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement.”

Putin told a press conference later that the three men had had a “free discussion” and a “mutual understanding” had taken place.

Some had hopes that the talks, which lasted about one hour and 20 minutes, could be used to discuss reductions in arms between the world’s three largest nuclear powers. Beijing has previously rebuffed advances by Trump to join such talks, pointing to the larger US and Russian stockpiles. On Thursday, though, Xi called for nuclear weapons to “be completely prohibited and thoroughly destroyed over time to make the world free of [them]”.

The language of the declaration around nuclear war is the same as that previously issued before by the five permanent members of the UN security council, which includes France and the UK. “The real test will be whether the three countries follow through on their stated commitment to discuss nuclear risk reduction and preventing nuclear proliferation,” said Patricia Kim, an expert on Chinese foreign policy at the Brookings Institution, a US thinktank. Even the suggestion that China would engage was significant, said Yun Sun, a senior fellow at the Stimson Center.

Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping pose for a photo at the first ever meeting of the leaders of the US, Russia and China. Photograph: Win McNamee/Getty Images AsiaPac/AP

Analysis

‘New page in history?’ Xi, Trump and Putin summit was more of a footnote

Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor

Far from the grand ambitions declared in Yalta in 1945, Shenzhen felt like a meeting in search of an agenda

• Apec summit – latest updates

It is arguably true, given it was the first such meeting of the leaders of China, Russia and the US, that Thursday’s gathering in Shenzhen deserved the description of “historic”.

But in terms of tangible outcomes, it is unlikely to warrant the “new page in the history of diplomacy” that Vladimir Putin claimed had been written, and will instead be consigned to a smallish footnote in any future volume of the 21st century.

It’s true that the meeting could yet be an icebreaker and the start of a permanent new dialogue. It’s also true that each leader can return home with something from the 90 minutes they spent together.

Despite falling asleep during the main Apec summit, Donald Trump had a chance to show his proximity to two authoritarian leaders he admires. With Ukraine having destroyed Russia’s bridge into Crimea, the US president greeted Putin not just as a friend but almost a wartime ally.

‘It’s my friend!’: Trump hails ‘great relationship’ with Putin at Apec summit – video

The Russian president, although occasionally pushed to one side by protocol during the early photo opportunities, will be able to show back home that it is Moscow, and not his adversary Europe, let alone Ukraine, that commands the respect and attention of Trump and his Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping. As such, the summit was a free gift to Putin, and underlined that Trump was no longer the leader of the free world, as the former British foreign secretary Jeremy Hunt commented.

From Putin’s perspective, a meeting in Berlin of the coalition of the willing was a sideshow. Europe’s attempts to isolate Russia had failed and the Asia-Pacific region had become the centre of the global economy, Putin boasted. His relationship with Trump, he said, despite the difficulties, was founded on “similar civilisational values”.

For Xi, it was a prestigious chance to play host, and implicitly demonstrate that the era of American hegemony is over. No longer the sole arbiter in world affairs, the US, the consumer economy, must share the stage with China, the manufacturing giant, and Russia, the energy bank.

Xi Jinping. Photograph: Sergey Bobylev/Sputnik/Kremlin pool/EPA

The trio’s brief joint statement covered four pretty disparate topics: boosting energy supply, reforming the United Nations, limiting the powers of the international criminal court (ICC) and a tentative commitment to discuss nuclear disarmament and non-proliferation.

For grandeur at a time of various global crises, these ambitions hardly matched Yalta in 1945 or even the declaration after the Tehran summit in 1943, when the leaders of the UK, US and Russia sat on the veranda of the British embassy and pledged that their countries would work together after the war to build a “world family of democratic nations” free of tyranny and oppression. Winston Churchill declaimed in Tehran: “In our hands we have the future of mankind.” Joseph Stalin went further. “History has spoiled us,” he said. “She has given us very great power and very great opportunities.”

Shenzhen by contrast felt like a meeting in search of an agenda. The vacuum was filled with platitudinous commitments to “maintain strategic stability and international security”, a task that – looking around the world – none of those in attendance are currently pursuing with great effect.

From left to right, Winston Churchill, Franklin Roosevelt and Joseph Stalin at the 1945 Yalta conference. Photograph: Universal Images Group/Getty Images

Perhaps technology, multipolarity and their own divisions means even they do not have “very great power”. Certainly there were no accompanying plans for how to reform the UN, let alone boost energy production or show respect for international law - a subject Trump’s current favoured successor, Marco Rubio, had just disparaged in a major speech as a plaything of the global elite.

Global courts under attack and four more takeaways from the Trump, Xi, Putin meeting

Read more

It was the summit’s chief instigator, Putin, who was the most eager of three to set the meeting in a historic context, describing China, Russia and the US as the victors of the second world war in a deliberate slight to Britain. A pledge to “preserve and strengthen the system of international law” seemingly referred to ensuring certain world leaders were freed from the prospect of the ICC serving them with arrest warrants.

By coincidence, the other world court – the international court of justice (ICJ) found a state – Myanmar – guilty of genocide for the first time on the same day. The Shenzen statement did not name the ICJ as a target beyond an oblique reference to the ICC and “other similar institutions”. Doubtless that is only because ICJ rulings can be dismissed with near impunity.

Xi, nervous that China’s status as protector of the global south might be damaged by being involved in a global superpower carve-up, stuck to a familiar script: “History tells us that when major powers are at peace, the world is secure. When they clash, there is chaos.”

It may be that behind the scenes, or at other events, serious progress is being made on how China might act as a guarantor of a peace deal with Iran, or on who should lead the UN through its coming phase of reform, or even on how Putin might bring himself to seek peace in Ukraine in a way that protects Ukrainian sovereignty.

For the moment though it looks as if what little history was made in Shenzhen was made for exclusively the wrong reasons.
