items.title: Trump, Putin and Xi release 'peace declaration' after historic meeting
items.summary: While the presidents have previously met for one-on-one meetings, this is their first trilateral discussion.
items.body:
Figure caption,

Trump greets 'my friend' Putin ahead of meeting with Xi

ByHarriet Whitehead

Updated 18 minutes ago

US President Donald Trump and his Russian and Chinese counterparts Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping have issued a "joint declaration of peace" following historic trilateral talks.

The three leaders met for 90 minutes in China's south-eastern city of Shenzhen, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.

While the presidents have previously had one-on-one meetings, these are their first trilateral talks.

In the declaration, they said "nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought" and that the countries planned to increase the production and supply of petroleum. They also said they were "committed to reform the UN" to respond more effectively to global challenges.

Thursday's statement also flagged the issue of immunity enjoyed by state officials and said "they agreed that the International Criminal Court and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction".

While in China, Trump also met Putin ahead of the trilateral, in their first meeting since August 2025, where the US president greeted his Russian counterpart as his "friend".

He also spoke with Xi in a separate conversation, describing the pair's relationship as "very special".

Beyond the warmth and shared niceties, however, the three men had different goals and motivations for the sit-down.

• This is a remarkable diplomatic moment for China's Xi - but it comes with pitfallsPublished10 hours ago

Image source, AFP via Getty Images

The opening remarks of the trilateral gave some indication about what was to be discussed during the closed-door meeting.

Before giving the floor to his fellow leaders, Xi said that "positive interaction among major powers is not a matter of choice, but a mandatory requirement".

Putin followed this by highlighting a shared interest in ending the Ukraine war and said the conversation would also touch on food and energy security.

China has officially remained neutral since Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, rejecting accusations from Kyiv and its allies that it has been tacitly supporting Moscow, including by exporting dual-use technology used by the Russian military.

Beijing has also repeatedly called for negotiations and a political settlement while avoiding condemnation of Russia's aggression.

Meanwhile, Trump closed by saying the presidents of three of the world's largest countries have a "special responsibility" to maintain productive dialogue.

"Too often past leaders have avoided talking to nations with whom they had disagreements," he said, adding: "We feel the opposite."

Trump referenced the three countries' nuclear capabilities and said they are "uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth".

It is "vital" that they co-operate to "combat the threat of nuclear proliferation in other countries around the world", he said, adding: "That's what we're doing in Iran."

"We're not going to let Iran have a nuclear weapon".

Trump then turned to Ukraine and said he and Putin have had a "long discussion" on the conflict there already.

He added that Putin "and I hope the other side, would like to see an end to that war".

Putin addressed the media following the trilateral meeting and described it as an "important chapter in the history of diplomacy".

He said Ukraine and Europe were not yet ready to make compromises to resolve the conflict in Ukraine - but he said Russia had invited EU representatives to Moscow to better understand Europe's position.

As the talks were under way in China, and even as Putin was holding his press conference claiming to be ready for peace, Ukraine's capital Kyiv was under attack from Russian drones.

Putin has repeatedly rejected all ceasefire offers from Ukraine, insisting on his maximalist demands which Kyiv and its European allies say are tantamount to de facto capitulation of Ukraine.

In Shenzhen, the Kremlin leader also vowed a "far more painful" retaliation in response to Ukrainian attacks on the bridge connecting Russia to Ukraine's occupied peninsula of Crimea. A missile and drone attack on Tuesday destroyed its central road section.

There was no mention from Putin of almost five years of Russian attacks on power plants, bridges and residential buildings in Ukraine.

The Russian president also directly addressed comparisons between his meeting with Trump and Xi and the 1945 Yalta Conference, where the leaders of the Soviet Union, Britain and the US met towards the end of World War Two.

"Nobody divided up the world at Yalta. It simply codified the realities that had emerged after WW2.

"And when it comes to today's conflicts, the realities on the ground will have to be accepted."

The Kremlin released a video showing Putin leaving the summit venue and saying goodbye to Xi.

"Thank you for organising this," Putin said. "I don't think anyone even expected everything to go so well."

Meanwhile, China's president described his meeting with Putin and Trump as "positive, constructive, and highly productive", according to the country's state broadcaster CCTV.

It added that Xi recalled "the history of fighting side-by-side during WW2", as the three leaders emphasised the importance of "cherishing the hard-won peace".

Thursday's trilateral meeting was reportedly the idea of Putin.

Some Russian newspapers called it a "diplomatic victory" as after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine many Western leaders were trying to isolate him.

The summit also marked the first time since Russia's war in Ukraine began that Putin took part in an international gathering attended by leaders from countries including Canada, Japan and Australia.

三位领导人在亚太经合组织（APEC）峰会期间，于中国东南部城市深圳举行了90分钟会晤。
虽然这几位总统此前有过一对一会晤，但这是他们的首次三边会谈。
在宣言中，他们表示“核战争打不赢，也绝不能打”，并称这些国家计划增加石油的生产和供应。他们还表示“致力于改革联合国”，以便更有效地应对全球挑战。
周四的声明还提到国家官员所享有的豁免权问题，并称“他们一致认为，国际刑事法院及其他类似机构不得滥用其管辖权”。
在华期间，特朗普还在三边会晤前会见了普京，这是两人自2025年8月以来的首次会晤，美国总统称这位俄罗斯同行是他的“朋友”。
他还与习近平单独交谈，称两人的关系“非常特别”。
然而，在热络气氛和客套之外，这三人对此次会晤各有不同的目标和动机。

items: 对中国的习近平而言，这是一个非凡的外交时刻——但也伴随着隐患。发布于10小时前

blocks.alt: US President Donald Trump (L) puts out his hand to shake hands with Russian President Vladimir Putin as China's President Xi Jinping looks on

blocks.text: 图片来源：AFP via Getty Images
三边会晤的开场发言，对闭门会议将讨论的内容给出了一些线索。
在请另外两位领导人发言之前，习近平说，“大国之间的良性互动不是可选项，而是必然要求”。
普京接着强调，结束乌克兰战争符合共同利益，并表示会谈也将涉及粮食和能源安全。
自普京2022年对乌克兰发动全面入侵以来，中国在官方上一直保持中立，并驳斥基辅及其盟友关于它一直在暗中支持莫斯科的指责，包括出口供俄军使用的两用技术。
北京也一再呼吁谈判和政治解决，同时避免谴责俄罗斯的侵略。
与此同时，特朗普在结束时表示，世界上最大的三个国家的总统，对保持富有成效的对话负有“特殊责任”。
“以往的领导人常常避免与存在分歧的国家对话，”他说，并补充道：“我们的想法正好相反。”
特朗普提到三国的核能力，称它们“处在讨论如何减少地球上核武器数量的独特位置”。
他说，他们合作“应对世界其他国家的核扩散威胁”是“至关重要的”，并补充道：“这正是我们在伊朗所做的。”
“我们不会让伊朗拥有核武器。”
特朗普随后谈到乌克兰，称他和普京已经就那里的冲突进行了“长时间讨论”。
他补充说，普京“而且我希望另一方也希望看到那场战争结束”。
普京在三边会晤后向媒体发表讲话，称这是“外交史上重要的一章”。
他说，乌克兰和欧洲尚未准备好作出妥协以解决乌克兰冲突——但他表示，俄罗斯已邀请欧盟代表前往莫斯科，以便更好地了解欧洲的立场。
会谈在中国进行之际，甚至就在普京举行新闻发布会声称已为和平做好准备时，乌克兰首都基辅正遭受俄罗斯无人机袭击。
普京一再拒绝乌克兰提出的所有停火建议，坚持其最高要价；基辅及其欧洲盟友称，这些要求无异于要乌克兰事实上投降。
在深圳，这位克里姆林宫领导人还誓言，将以“痛苦得多”的报复回应乌克兰对连接俄罗斯与其占领的克里米亚半岛大桥的袭击。周二的导弹和无人机袭击摧毁了该桥的中央公路段。
普京只字未提近五年来俄罗斯对乌克兰发电厂、桥梁和居民楼的袭击。
这位俄罗斯总统还直接回应了将他与特朗普、习近平的会晤同1945年雅尔塔会议相提并论的说法——第二次世界大战临近结束时，苏联、英国和美国领导人曾在那里会面。
“没有人在雅尔塔瓜分世界。它只是把第二次世界大战后已经形成的现实以条文固定下来。
“而谈到当今的冲突，必须接受当地的现实。”
克里姆林宫发布视频，显示普京离开峰会会场并与习近平道别。
“感谢你组织这次会晤，”普京说。“我想谁都没料到一切会进行得这么顺利。”
与此同时，据中国官方媒体CCTV报道，中国国家主席称他与普京和特朗普的会晤“积极、建设性且富有成效”。
报道还称，习近平回顾了“第二次世界大战期间并肩作战的历史”，三位领导人强调了“珍惜来之不易的和平”的重要性。
据称周四的三边会晤是普京提出的。
一些俄罗斯报纸称之为“外交胜利”，因为在俄罗斯全面入侵乌克兰后，许多西方领导人曾试图孤立他。
此次峰会也是自俄罗斯对乌克兰开战以来，普京首次参加有加拿大、日本和澳大利亚等国领导人出席的国际聚会。

items.summary: Andy Burnham due in Brussels on Friday but sticking points on food rules and tuition fees remain unresolved The UK-EU reset talks will go “down to the wire” as the British government battles to have a say in shaping future European food and farming rules. With less than 24 hours to go before Andy Bu…
items.body:
Andy Burnham with Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, at the UN general assembly in New York in September. Photograph: WPA/Getty Images

Andy Burnham with Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, at the UN general assembly in New York in September. Photograph: WPA/Getty Images

UK-EU reset talks will go ‘down to the wire’ as crunch summit approaches

Andy Burnham due in Brussels on Friday but sticking points on food rules and tuition fees remain unresolved

The UK-EU reset talks will go “down to the wire” as the British government battles to have a say in shaping future European food and farming rules.

With less than 24 hours to go before Andy Burnham is due in Brussels for a summit with EU leaders, the two sides still need to resolve some key sticking points, including how much of a say Britain will have in new EU food rules.

“It will go down to the wire,” an EU diplomat said, speaking in general terms about the disagreements, including tuition fees. “Our feeling is that the Brits have to move if they want a deal.”

A spokesperson for the British prime minister also described the talks as close, saying if an agreement was reached, the government would bring forward legislation, the cutting costs bill, to parliament next week.

The Guardian view on Europe and Burnham: a future that can only be viewed through a glass darkly | Editorial

Read more

Another EU diplomat said ambassadors representing the EU member states would meet at 5pm and “will go until agreement is reached tonight”.

Sources said the UK was still resisting pressure from the EU to agree to working on tuition fees for EU students coming to the UK under a new youth mobility scheme.

“We are fighting hard on this and think we will get there,” said an EU insider. “But for us, one of the hardest discussions centres on this question of the UK being a rule taker or rule maker.”

At the long-awaited summit, the EU and UK hope to sign three agreements, including a highly prized food and drink deal that was a Labour manifesto commitment and is expected to add 0.4% to British GDP.

The deal, expected to come into force on 1 March 2028, requires the UK to align with EU rules on sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) standards, making Britain a rule taker.

Asked about Britain’s status as a rule taker, No 10 said the Labour manifesto had aimed to build closer ties with the EU. “We were obviously elected on a manifesto that promised to reset the relationship and seek to deepen ties with our European friends,” it said.

According to EU sources, the UK has been pushing to have a formal role in EU committees involved in implementing existing and setting new SPS rules.

But after a meeting of EU ambassadors that ended late on Wednesday, the issue remained unresolved. The EU diplomat said: “They want to be able to shape decisions, not only implementation, but future decisions. That has always been a red line.”

Under the SPS proposal, the UK will agree to dynamically align with EU laws and will have a “voice” but “not be in the room” when laws are drafted.

A second diplomat from a country sympathetic to the British position said the European Commission had proposed an “extremely restrictive consultation mechanism” for the UK.

In contrast, the EU diplomat thought it was reasonable for a British representative to take part in the implementation of SPS legislation affecting the UK.

“Of course the UK cannot vote in the council as a non-member state, but we feel that we need to be pragmatic about coordination and implementation,” they said.

after newsletter promotion

The issue raises the tensions at the heart of the UK’s status as a rule taker, and would be many times magnified were Britain to choose to enter the single market as a non-EU member state.

The precise details of how the UK would be consulted on future food and farming rules remain unclear.

Separately, the EU and UK remain deadlocked over whether EU students in Britain should pay the British or international rate of university tuition, and the overall numbers who could take part in the scheme.

The draft proposal gives the UK two options: to agree to significantly reduced undergraduate fees or equal treatment with nationals.

Burnham’s spokesperson suggested there was an UK-EU consensus that there would be no further incremental reset summits beyond the one on Friday until a full negotiation commenced on a longer term, more stable relationship, such as rejoining the single market.

“After the summit, we will begin those discussions with our European partners about the realistic options for our longer-term relationship,” he said.

The UK has prioritised seeking commitments on Britain’s position relating to the EU’s Made in Europe legislation. The trade defence policy will include tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles but will also affect British manufacturing. The sides are believed to be close to an agreement to language at the summit that would point towards UK inclusion, but nothing can be formalised until the EU passes its own legislation.

Burnham’s spokesperson said: “[The UK is] engaging constructively with the EU on that, and we’ve been clear about the challenges it could represent for British industries. We have deeply integrated supply chains with Europe, and we want to keep working together to boost growth and open up trade.

“The UK and Europe have shared economic challenges, and we believe shared challenges are best met with a collective approach that is in Britain’s best interests, and in Europe’s too.”

items.title: Trump takes 500 actions to weaken cancer protections, new report says
items.summary: Natural Resources Defense Council shows how federal rules changes will increase public’s exposure to carcinogens Amid a rise in early onset cancer , the Trump administration has taken more than 500 actions to systematically dismantle protections against carcinogens once in place across the federal g…
items.body:
A rancher watches as a rig helps replug one of the abandoned wells at her ranch near Crane, Texas, in July 2021. Some of the wells were leaking carcinogenic chemicals into the fields and drinking water. Photograph: Eric Gay/AP

A rancher watches as a rig helps replug one of the abandoned wells at her ranch near Crane, Texas, in July 2021. Some of the wells were leaking carcinogenic chemicals into the fields and drinking water. Photograph: Eric Gay/AP

Trump takes 500 actions to weaken cancer protections, new report says

Natural Resources Defense Council shows how federal rules changes will increase public’s exposure to carcinogens

Amid a rise in early onset cancer, the Trump administration has taken more than 500 actions to systematically dismantle protections against carcinogens once in place across the federal government, an October report alleges.

The Natural Resources Defense Council report, and comments from current and former officials from the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), brings into focus how myriad changes in federal rules or protocol will dramatically increase the public’s exposure to carcinogens. These are taking effect at a time when some forms of early onset cancer are spiking by about 30% per decade.

Some of the changes have drawn widespread outrage and backlash, including the administration delaying new protections around asbestos, or siding with Bayer in its fight to keep glyphosate, classified as a probable human carcinogen by an arm of the World Health Organization in 2015, on the market.

But most changes lie in the nuts and bolts of the federal government. These include alterations to important scientific processes that determine the level of risk people face in exposure to carcinogens. With a few minor adjustments, once-problematic levels of exposure to carcinogens, such as formaldehyde, are no longer considered a danger in the federal government’s eyes.

Cancer rates rising more quickly among younger people, international research finds

Read more

Other actions include the elimination of protective regulatory rules, the exploitation of presidential exemptions for polluters, the delay of new regulations already in motion, the elimination of research funding and wide-scale cuts to cancer research staff.

The actions amount to a “pro-cancer” agenda, the report states. NRDC lead author Erik Olson said he was “surprised by the breadth of the whole government effort to undermine all the protections against cancer”. It is not just the EPA, Olson said, but the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, the Occupational Safety and Health Administration, independent commissions and many other governmental entities.

“The vast majority of people have no idea that this is happening because the Trump administration is mostly doing it without a lot of fanfare, so it’s hard to piece together this jigsaw puzzle, but we did and it shows a stark and shocking picture,” Olson said.

A White House spokesperson, Allison Schuster, said: “Make America Healthy Again was not just a campaign slogan – it was President Trump’s pledge to tackle America’s chronic disease epidemic.

“Delivering on this pledge has been a whole-of-government effort, and the White House’s launch of MAHA.gov transparently documents the Administration’s progress so far. President Trump will never stop fighting to empower Americans to take control of their health.”

An EPA spokesperson said the administration had delivered more than 500 environmental wins so far.

“The Trump EPA, as it has been since day one, is fully committed to fulfilling its core mission of protecting human health and the environment and has put the gold standard of science at every action it takes,” a spokesperson said.

Officials estimate there will be more than 2m US cancer diagnoses this year. People younger than 50 years old have experienced a nearly 3% increase in colon cancer rates each year from 2013 to 2022. More broadly, rates for 14 types of common cancers have jumped in recent decades, including a 35% increase in childhood leukemia.

The situation calls for more protections, but those rules, regulations and scientific processes that are most essential have long been on industry’s hitlist, said an EPA employee who declined to use their name for fear of retribution. Former industry officials are now running the EPA, and it is “horrifying to watch it all play out”, the employee said.

“It is coming from the top [of the agency], and they are being methodical, and doing a lot of damage to these very critical protection points, which is exactly what the chemical industry has wanted,” the employee said. “There is no way to sugarcoat what is happening.”

Among the most widely reverberating changes is the shift away from the “no safe level of exposure” principle that guided EPA science in developing protections for carcinogens. This works by assuming any level of exposure to carcinogens presents a risk, and the risk grows as the exposure dose grows.

The Trump EPA has started implementing a “threshold” approach in which it determines that some exposures to carcinogens is safe. This change has already resulted in weaker protections against formaldehyde, a toxicant widely used in consumer goods. The administration appears to be taking a similar approach to its regulation of hexavalent chromium, a widespread water contaminant.

Nuclear regulators are also eliminating the obligation to reduce exposure to radioactive carcinogens to the lowest reasonably achievable level, despite decades of scientific evidence that any level of radiation poses a cancer risk, the report states.

David Fotouhi, the second in command at the EPA, wrote in an early 2026 memo that the agency had been too conservative in estimating toxic chemicals’ health risks, including carcinogenicity. Those values should be revisited and loosened, Fatouhi suggested.

This undermines work on 500 risk assessments done since 1985 by the Integrated Risk Information System (Iris), the small EPA office that determines chemical toxicity. The changes to risk assessments are among the most pernicious Trump EPA moves because the findings underpin regulations that protect people from carcinogens in the air, water, consumer goods and elsewhere, said Betsy Southerland, a former water office director at the agency.

The change to the threshold approach is part of that, and the agency is also targeting a mechanism that protects children by factoring in an increased risk in their exposure to chemicals.

“This is a killer for any emerging contaminant work, and for [carcinogens and other chemicals] that they are revisiting,” Southerland said. The changes could also weaken cleanup requirements at Superfund sites, which is the designation for the nation’s most polluted areas, many of which contain cancer-linked substances.

In latest blow to Obamacare, Trump is threatening the entire US health system

Read more

The Trump EPA quietly loosened guidance around the type of studies required to set regulations around carcinogens, the report alleges. Long-term human or animal studies are the norm, but the agency now uses short-term modeling studies called new approach methodologies (Nams) that are known to be unreliable and easy to manipulate. A Nam study was used to weaken the risk assessment for p-DCB, a widely used consumer chemical that most regulatory agencies label a carcinogen.

Trump has also dramatically increased the use of “presidential pardons” for carcinogenic air pollution, which the report claims will increase exposure to arsenic, ethylene oxide and similar carcinogenic chemicals.

Meanwhile, the agency appears to be systematically using stall tactics via multiple channels to grind the regulatory process to a halt. For example, it delayed requirements for industry to provide cancer data for carcinogenic chemicals including benzene, bisphenol A and vinyl chloride, the building block for PVC material, which were supposed to be reviewed during the administration. It is unclear when this will happen.

Olson likened the situation to someone “dumping a huge dump truck full of termites on your house”.

“It’s not like any one termite is causing the house to collapse, but this is a totally intentional strategy of having innumerable termites eating away at the foundation of all our protections, and the house is going to collapse,” Olson said.

The situation calls for more protections, but those rules, regulations and scientific processes that are most essential have long been on industry’s hitlist, said an EPA employee who declined to use their name for fear of retribution. Former industry officials are now running the EPA, and it is “horrifying to watch it all play out”, the employee said.

“It is coming from the top [of the agency], and they are being methodical, and doing a lot of damage to these very critical protection points, which is exactly what the chemical industry has wanted,” the employee said. “There is no way to sugarcoat what is happening.”

Among the most widely reverberating changes is the shift away from the “no safe level of exposure” principle that guided EPA science in developing protections for carcinogens. This works by assuming any level of exposure to carcinogens presents a risk, and the risk grows as the exposure dose grows.

The Trump EPA has started implementing a “threshold” approach in which it determines that some exposures to carcinogens is safe. This change has already resulted in weaker protections against formaldehyde, a toxicant widely used in consumer goods. The administration appears to be taking a similar approach to its regulation of hexavalent chromium, a widespread water contaminant.

Nuclear regulators are also eliminating the obligation to reduce exposure to radioactive carcinogens to the lowest reasonably achievable level, despite decades of scientific evidence that any level of radiation poses a cancer risk, the report states.

David Fotouhi, the second in command at the EPA, wrote in an early 2026 memo that the agency had been too conservative in estimating toxic chemicals’ health risks, including carcinogenicity. Those values should be revisited and loosened, Fatouhi suggested.

This undermines work on 500 risk assessments done since 1985 by the Integrated Risk Information System (Iris), the small EPA office that determines chemical toxicity. The changes to risk assessments are among the most pernicious Trump EPA moves because the findings underpin regulations that protect people from carcinogens in the air, water, consumer goods and elsewhere, said Betsy Southerland, a former water office director at the agency.
The change to the threshold approach is part of that, and the agency is also targeting a mechanism that protects children by factoring in an increased risk in their exposure to chemicals.

“This is a killer for any emerging contaminant work, and for [carcinogens and other chemicals] that they are revisiting,” Southerland said. The changes could also weaken cleanup requirements at Superfund sites, which is the designation for the nation’s most polluted areas, many of which contain cancer-linked substances.
In latest blow to Obamacare, Trump is threatening the entire US health system
Read more

The Trump EPA quietly loosened guidance around the type of studies required to set regulations around carcinogens, the report alleges. Long-term human or animal studies are the norm, but the agency now uses short-term modeling studies called new approach methodologies (Nams) that are known to be unreliable and easy to manipulate. A Nam study was used to weaken the risk assessment for p-DCB, a widely used consumer chemical that most regulatory agencies label a carcinogen.

Trump has also dramatically increased the use of “presidential pardons” for carcinogenic air pollution, which the report claims will increase exposure to arsenic, ethylene oxide and similar carcinogenic chemicals.

Meanwhile, the agency appears to be systematically using stall tactics via multiple channels to grind the regulatory process to a halt. For example, it delayed requirements for industry to provide cancer data for carcinogenic chemicals including benzene, bisphenol A and vinyl chloride, the building block for PVC material, which were supposed to be reviewed during the administration. It is unclear when this will happen.
Olson likened the situation to someone “dumping a huge dump truck full of termites on your house”.

“It’s not like any one termite is causing the house to collapse, but this is a totally intentional strategy of having innumerable termites eating away at the foundation of all our protections, and the house is going to collapse,” Olson said.

2021年7月，一名牧场主在得克萨斯州克兰附近的牧场上，看着一台钻机协助重新封堵废弃油井。其中一些油井当时正在向田地和饮用水中泄漏致癌化学品。照片：Eric Gay/AP
新报告称，特朗普采取500项行动削弱癌症防护
自然资源保护协会指出，联邦规则变更将增加公众对致癌物的暴露
一份十月份的报告指控，在早发癌症上升之际，特朗普政府已采取500多项行动，系统性地拆除联邦政府原先针对致癌物的保护措施。
自然资源保护协会的报告，以及环保署（EPA）现任和前任官员的评论，揭示了联邦规则或程序中的诸多变化将如何大幅增加公众对致癌物的暴露。这些变化正在生效，而与此同时，某些早发癌症的发病率每十年约上升30%。
其中一些变化已引发广泛愤怒和反弹，包括政府推迟围绕石棉的新保护措施，或在拜耳为保住草甘膦（2015年被世界卫生组织下属机构列为对人类很可能致癌）市场地位的抗争中站在拜耳一边。
但大多数变化发生在联邦政府的具体运作环节。其中包括对判定人们接触致癌物所面临风险水平的重要科学程序作出改动。只需稍作调整，曾经成问题的致癌物暴露水平——例如甲醛——在联邦政府看来便不再被视为危险。
国际研究发现，年轻人中的癌症发病率上升更快
阅读更多
其他行动还包括取消保护性监管规则、利用总统豁免为污染者开脱、拖延已经在推进的新规、取消研究资金，以及大规模裁减癌症研究人员。
报告称，这些行动相当于一项“亲癌症”议程。自然资源保护协会报告的首席作者埃里克·奥尔森说，他“对整个政府为削弱所有抗癌保护所做努力的广度感到惊讶”。奥尔森说，这不只是环保署，还有疾病控制与预防中心、核管理委员会、职业安全与健康管理局、各独立委员会以及许多其他政府机构。
奥尔森说：“绝大多数人根本不知道这件事正在发生，因为特朗普政府大多在没有大张旗鼓的情况下推进，所以很难把这幅拼图拼起来，但我们拼出来了，呈现的是一幅严峻而令人震惊的图景。”
白宫发言人艾莉森·舒斯特说：“‘让美国重新健康’（Make America Healthy Again）不只是一句竞选口号——这是特朗普总统应对美国慢性病流行的承诺。
“兑现这一承诺是一项全政府的努力，白宫上线的 MAHA.gov 透明地记录了本届政府迄今的进展。特朗普总统将永不停止奋斗，以赋能美国人掌控自己的健康。”
美国环保署发言人说，本届政府迄今已取得500多项环境方面的成果。
发言人说：“特朗普治下的环保署从第一天起就全力履行保护人类健康和环境的核心使命，并在它所采取的每一项行动中都采用了黄金标准的科学。”
官员估计，今年美国将有超过200万例癌症诊断。50岁以下人群的结肠癌发病率在2013年至2022年间几乎每年上升近3%。更广泛地看，14种常见癌症的发病率近几十年来大幅上升，其中包括儿童白血病上升了35%。
一名因担心遭到报复而不愿具名的环保署员工说，这种局面需要更多保护，但那些最为关键的规则、条例和科学程序，长期以来一直在产业界的打击名单上。如今前产业界官员掌管着环保署，这名员工说，“看着这一切上演令人恐惧”。
这名员工说：“这是从（该机构）高层下来的，他们手法系统，正在对这些极其关键的保护节点造成大量损害，而这正是化工行业一直想要的。发生的事情没有办法粉饰。”
影响最为广泛的变化之一，是偏离了指导环保署科学制定致癌物保护措施的“不存在安全暴露水平”原则。该原则假定，任何水平的致癌物暴露都存在风险，且风险随暴露剂量增加而增大。
特朗普治下的环保署已开始实施“阈值”方法，认定对致癌物的某些暴露是安全的。这一变化已经导致对甲醛（一种广泛用于消费品的有毒物质）的保护被削弱。政府似乎也在以类似方式监管六价铬这种广泛存在的水污染物。
报告称，核监管机构也在取消将放射性致癌物暴露降至合理可达最低水平的义务，尽管数十年来的科学证据表明，任何水平的辐射都存在致癌风险。
环保署二把手 David Fotouhi 在 2026 年初的一份备忘录中写道，该机构在估算有毒化学品的健康风险（包括致癌性）时过于保守。Fatouhi 建议应重新审视并放宽这些数值。
这削弱了自1985年以来由综合风险信息系统（Iris）完成的500项风险评估工作，Iris是环保署内负责判定化学品毒性的一个小型部门。前该机构水务办公室主任贝齐·萨瑟兰说，对风险评估的改动是特朗普治下环保署最恶劣的举措之一，因为这些结论是保护人们免受空气、水、消费品及其他环境中致癌物伤害的法规基础。
改为阈值方法是其中一部分，该机构还在针对一项保护儿童的机制，该机制会把儿童接触化学品的更高风险考虑在内。
萨瑟兰说：“这对任何新兴污染物工作，以及对他们正在重新审视的（致癌物和其他化学品）来说都是致命打击。”这些变化还可能削弱超级基金（Superfund）场地的清理要求。超级基金是对全国污染最严重地区的认定，其中许多场地含有与癌症相关的物质。
奥巴马医保再遭打击，特朗普正威胁整个美国医疗体系
阅读更多
报告指控，特朗普治下的环保署悄悄放宽了制定致癌物监管规则所需研究类型的指南。长期人体或动物研究本是常规做法，但该机构现在使用被称为新方法学（Nams）的短期模型研究，这类研究被认为不可靠且易于操纵。一项 Nam 研究被用来削弱对 p-DCB 的风险评估，这是一种被大多数监管机构列为致癌物、广泛使用的消费化学品。
特朗普还大幅增加了对致癌空气污染使用“总统赦免”的做法，该报告称这将增加人们接触砷、环氧乙烷及类似致癌化学品的机会。
与此同时，该机构似乎在通过多种渠道系统性地使用拖延战术，使监管进程陷入停滞。例如，它推迟了要求业界为包括苯、双酚A和氯乙烯（PVC材料的基本构件）在内的致癌化学品提供癌症数据的要求，而这些数据本应在本届政府任内接受审查。目前尚不清楚这将何时进行。
奥尔森将这一局面比作有人“把满满一大卡车白蚁倒在你家房子上”。
奥尔森说：“并不是某一只白蚁导致房子倒塌，但这是一种完全有意的策略：让无数白蚁啃噬我们所有保护措施的根基，房子就会倒塌。”

The Aria CEO, Annabelle Herd, says the music industry won’t desert other creatives: ‘We stand with the rest of the creative and media industries.’ Photograph: Wendell Teodoro/Getty Images

The Aria CEO, Annabelle Herd, says the music industry won’t desert other creatives: ‘We stand with the rest of the creative and media industries.’ Photograph: Wendell Teodoro/Getty Images

Australian music industry rejects ‘divide and conquer’ proposal to give musicians exemption from AI scraping

Reported proposal to give musicians special treatment is ‘unworkable’, Aria CEO says, vowing to stand with other creatives

• Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast

The music industry will not accept an AI carveout deal that leaves other creative sectors behind, rejecting a reported proposal to give musicians special treatment while allowing big tech to train on other copyrighted material – described by David Pocock as a “divide and conquer strategy”.

The trade union representing writers and creatives is “alarmed” at a proposal to let AI companies train on Australian data if they buy a permit, an idea also strongly rebuffed by the Coalition and Greens.

The Albanese government would not comment on the reported proposal, but senior ministers have raised concerns about current copyright law in recent days, hinting reforms were needed.

Annabelle Herd, the CEO of the Australian Recording Industry Association (Aria), and Claire Pullen, the CEO of the Australian Writers’ Guild, said the creative community – which this week launched a major AI campaign – would remain united in rejecting such changes.

“I can’t see any creative workers leaving their colleagues behind,” Pullen said.

Elton John backs Australian artists in fight against AI in surprise Aria awards appearance

Read more

The Australian Financial Review reported on Thursday the government was considering a copyright change under which AI companies would buy permits to train on Australian content, but that music may be exempted. Such a proposal would be more in line with AI companies, after Anthropic suggested a model of “conditional approval” to scrape content unless a rightsholder objected, and OpenAI told a parliamentary committee it would “potentially” support paying into a fund for creators.

• Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

Guardian Australia was not able to independently verify details of the proposal. One senior member of the creative community, involved in copyright discussions with government, said they had heard some details of such an idea, but others said they had not and doubted the Albanese government would seriously entertain it. One source in the AI industry, who declined to be named, said they would welcome such a plan.

Aria awards: how do Australian artists feel about their music being used to train AI? – video

Herd said she was unaware of the proposal before Thursday, but the music industry would not desert other creatives.

“Had we been consulted, we would have advised this scheme is unnecessary, unworkable and designed to suit the commercial interests of AI companies, not protect creators,” she told Guardian Australia.

“Our position is unchanged: we stand with the rest of the creative and media industries.”

Herd and Pullen said such a scheme would be difficult to implement technically, questioning how content like movies or TV shows – which combine copyrighted elements such as music, video and screenwriting – would be treated if just one element was exempted from AI scraping.

“This just seems like such a convoluted path, when AI companies have had an open invitation to sit down and negotiate for years. We have been working with government to come up with a model since 2024. We’ve come up with solutions and tech has steadfastly refused to even talk,” Pullen said.

While the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, has declared it would be “theft” if creatives weren’t paid for their work, and that artists “need to be compensated”, some AI companies have argued it is too difficult to make individual licensing deals under existing copyright law.

The Media, Entertainment & Arts Alliance said it would be “alarmed” at the reported proposal, and demanded protections promised by Albanese “must apply to all creative sectors”.

Weakening AI copyright law will spell ‘disaster for creativity’, global music body warns Albanese

Read more

While government MPs declined to comment on the report, senior Labor figures have recently begun more forcefully pointing to what they claim are shortfalls in copyright law in the AI age – despite major rightsholder groups rejecting the need for change. The industry minister, Tim Ayres, on Tuesday said “the status quo is no good” for creative workers, a line repeated by the acting prime minister, Richard Marles, on Thursday. Marles added on News24: “People are being ripped off”.

The attorney general, Michelle Rowland, also used newly strengthened language when contacted, promising “certainty and strong protections for Australian artists”.

“Right now, the work of Australian creatives is being used without their consent or payment,” a spokesperson for Rowland said.

“The Government has long advocated for tech companies to strike commercial deals with Australian artists, and we will continue to do so.”

Potentially carving out musicians did not win support among parliamentarians, either.

The shadow attorney general, Michaelia Cash, claimed such a proposal would “divide the rightsholders”.

“This ham-fisted tactic should be strongly resisted. Everyone who owns property should have the same right for it not to be stolen.”

Pocock also described it as “some sort of divide and conquer strategy”.

“It’s hard to know what [Labor] are actually doing at the moment. The joint select committee hasn’t even given its report to the government, and we’re hearing all sorts of whispers about what the government is planning.”

Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young urged the government not to meet copyright demands requested by big tech.

“What they’re asking Australia to do actually is to undermine copyright the world over. Australia will become known as the Cayman Islands for AI if we allow this loophole to happen,” she told News24.

“I say, don’t be that stupid. Stand up to them.”

她对《卫报》澳大利亚版表示：“如果事先征求我们的意见，我们会指出这项方案既无必要、也行不通，而且是为了迎合人工智能公司的商业利益，而不是保护创作者。”

司法部长米歇尔·罗兰在接受询问时也使用了力度更强的措辞，承诺“为澳大利亚艺术家提供确定性与有力保护”。

“政府长期以来一直主张科技公司与澳大利亚艺术家达成商业协议，我们将继续这样做。”
将音乐人单独豁免的设想，在议员中也未赢得支持。
影子司法部长米凯莉娅·卡什声称，这样的提案会“分裂权利人”。

Prof Matthew Davis, Dr Charles Woffinden and Prof Andrew White of the University of Queensland, pictured inside the elevator they used to send a message via gravitational communication. Photograph: University of Queensland

An elevator, a brick wall and a bathroom: scientists use gravity to send ‘practically unblockable’ message

Australian physicists chose to transmit the word ‘gravity’ in binary code through brick wall

• Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Australian scientists have used gravity as a means of communication, in a proof-of-concept experiment involving a snail-paced 1950s elevator, a brick wall and a men’s bathroom.

Physicists at the University of Queensland have used gravity to transmit a “practically unblockable” message about 70cm through a brick wall, by sending an elevator up and down between two floors and measuring changes in the gravitational field as a result of the movement.

From gold rush to cosmic questions: a South Dakota mine and the search for the secrets of the universe

Read more

The research, published in the journal Science Advances, involved a sensitive detection device known as a gravimeter, which was set up on the floor of a men’s bathroom adjacent to the lift.

The gravimeter was able to detect the position of the elevator’s 1.8-tonne counterweight as it moved between two levels – representing 0 and 1 in binary code – which enabled the scientists to send a message.

A gravimeter, set up in a men’s bathroom, was used to detect the position of an elevator counterweight, enabling scientists to transmit a message. Photograph: Andrew Groszek/University of Queensland

The researchers chose to transmit the word “gravity”, or 1000111 1110010 1100001 1110110 1101001 1110100 1111001 in binary code. At a transmission rate of one bit (digit) per minute, the single word took nearly an hour to send.

The scientists say that while gravitational communication is currently far from usable given its extremely slow speed, an advantage is that it is a “practically unblockable wireless communication scheme”.

“Unlike the electromagnetic signals used in modern wireless communication, a gravitational signal cannot simply be screened out by placing ordinary material in its path,” said co-author Dr Charles Woffinden, of UQ’s school of mathematics and physics, in a statement. “Anyone who has lost phone reception in a tunnel or struggled with wifi through a solid wall will understand the appeal.”

Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email

Study co-author Prof Matthew Davis told Guardian Australia: “At the moment, it’s very hard to imagine how it could be practically useful.” But he added that the experiment was “theoretically interesting enough that it was worth doing”.

To put into perspective how slow the message transmission was, Davis said that Nasa’s Voyager 1 spacecraft, which after 49 years of travel had just reached a distance of one light-day away, could “communicate with Earth at a faster data rate than our communication concept”.

According to Davis, the new method of communicating could theoretically occur at ranges of up to 500 metres and at a rate 15 times faster, if more sensitive quantum gravity sensors were used.

‘It’s literally slower than watching Australia drift north’: the laboratory experiment that will outlive us all

Read more

The idea for the elevator study arose from a project to develop a contactless weighbridge – which would use quantum sensors to detect changes in the strength of gravity due to a passing truck, allowing scientists to determine the mass of a large vehicle.

Classical gravimeters can be thought of as a mass on a spring. “If you stretch the spring, the mass bounces up and down at a certain rate, which is determined by the spring and the gravitational field,” Davis said. “If the gravitational field changes ever so slightly, the rate at which it bounces back and forth changes.”

“Quantum sensors are still under development,” Davis said.

“Sometimes doing physics leads in unexpected ways and it’s a bit of fun … you get to do quirky things on the side,” he added. “It’s one of the great joys of science to have stuff like this happen.”

Other near-unblockable methods of communication – involving neutrinos or gravitational waves – have been proposed, “but these approaches are somewhat hindered by the difficulty in generating a measurable signal”, the scientists note.

The physicists conducted the research in UQ’s Parnell physics building, which is also home to the world’s longest-running science experiment – the pitch drop experiment, which began in 1927.

items.title: Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya minority, world’s top court rules
items.summary: Judgment finds ‘intent to destroy a substantial part of the Rohingya population’ after case seen as critical test for dealing with most serious of state crimes Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority during a 2017 military campaign, the world’s highest court has ruled, in a historic…
items.body:
A man helps Rohingya Muslim refugees to disembark from a boat on the Bangladeshi shoreline of the Naf River after crossing the border from Myanmar in September 2017. Photograph: Fred Dufour/AFP/Getty Images

A man helps Rohingya Muslim refugees to disembark from a boat on the Bangladeshi shoreline of the Naf River after crossing the border from Myanmar in September 2017. Photograph: Fred Dufour/AFP/Getty Images

Myanmar committed acts of genocide against Rohingya minority, world’s top court rules

Judgment ends seven-year legal battle and is seen as critical test for dealing with most serious of all state crimes

Myanmar committed acts of genocide against its Rohingya minority during “clearance operations” nearly a decade ago, the world’s highest court has ruled.

The judgment from the international court of justice (ICJ) – which has never previously found a state responsible for genocide – ends a seven-year legal battle and is seen as a critical global test for dealing with the most serious of all state crimes.

“The court is fully convinced that Myanmar committed acts falling under … the genocide convention with an intent to destroy a substantial part of the Rohingya population in Myanmar,” the ICJ president, Yuji Iwasawa, said during a reading of the judgment.

A 2016-17 campaign by Myanmar’s military forced more than 700,000 mostly Muslim Rohingya to flee across the border into Bangladesh, with refugees arriving with stories of mass killings of adults and children, gang-rapes and burned-down villages.

Governments have been anxiously awaiting the decision, handed down in The Hague, the Netherlands, where the UN-run court is based, in part because the ruling will set a precedent for genocide claims, notably a high-profile case against Israel.

Genocide, defined after the Nazi Holocaust by a 1948 UN convention, is harder to prove than war crimes because it requires evidence of specific “intent” to destroy a national, ethnical, racial or religious group.

Myanmar’s case was raised by the Gambia, a Muslim-majority state, on behalf of Myanmar survivors. It rested on claims of genocidal statements and “patterns of conduct” that showed attempts to destroy the group during assaults on Rakhine state, including gunning down people as they fled and blocking their return.

In January, the ICJ held closed-door sessions to hear from survivors who travelled from camps in Bangladesh. More than 1 million Rohingya still live there in the world’s largest refugee settlement, and fewer than 600,000 are estimated to remain in Buddhist-majority Myanmar.

Mumtaz Begum, pictured in 2017 in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh. She fled to Bangladesh shortly after an attack on Tula Toli village in Myanmar, in which she said the military burned homes, gang-raped women and killed her husband and son in front of her. Photograph: Allison Joyce/Getty Images

Refugees who fled to Bangladesh told the Guardian in 2017 of a massacre in the village of Tula Toli, where survivors described systematic shooting of civilians, mass graves and the drowning of children in a river. That village, which satellite footage later showed had been burned down, was one of several analysed by rights investigators and built a case for genocide.

During hearings, the Gambian justice minister, Dawda Jallow, told the court the case was not “about esoteric issues of international law”.

“It is about real people, real stories and a real group of human beings,” said Jallow. “The Rohingya of Myanmar. They have been targeted for destruction.”

Legal experts see Thursday’s judgment as a key test for sexual violence in genocide assessments, as the convention says the crime can include acts with the intent to “prevent births”. Investigators have said gang-rapes and accounts of soldiers mutilating women’s genitals were carried out intentionally and systematically to stop reproduction.

Myanmar denied carrying out a genocide and claims its actions targeted a Rohingya militant group that conducted guerrilla-style attacks. Its military responded with massive “clearance operations”.

The country’s leader, Min Aung Hlaing, who headed the military during the 2016-2017 attacks, has a pending arrest warrant from the international criminal court (ICC), which prosecutes individuals and not states like the ICJ, on allegations of crimes against humanity.

Bangladeshi guards stand by as thousands of Rohingya refugees fleeing from Myanmar walk along a muddy rice field after crossing the border in Palang Khali, Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh. Photograph: Paula Bronstein/Getty Images

The former general overthrew the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi in a 2021 coup, triggering a civil war that has left tens of thousands dead. He was installed as civilian president in April after elections that were widely discredited.

While the ICJ does not have the power to enforce rulings, its decisions are considered binding, carry diplomatic weight and can shape international action, including sanctions.

Israel and its chief ally, the US, have been closely following the Myanmar case as the decision provides the strongest hint of how judges might assess the Gaza case, brought by South Africa. UN independent investigations, as well as genocide scholars, have already said Israel committed acts of genocide in Gaza.

A judgment finding Myanmar had breached the convention has been predicted to lead to the US imposing sanctions on ICJ judges, including this year’s Nobel peace prize winner, Navi Pillay.

A Myanmar border guard police stands near a fence, behind which are Rohingya refugees and makeshift houses at the ‘no man’s land’ zone between the Bangladesh-Myanmar border in Rakhine State, western Myanmar, in 2018. Photograph: Nyein Chan Naing/EPA

Washington had considered the Rohingya crisis to be a genocide, based on a decision by the Biden administration. However, the Trump administration has been on the offensive against international rights bodies, including imposing sanctions on the ICC.

Two other ICJ cases dealing with atrocities in the 1990s Balkans wars fell short of finding states directly responsible for genocide, although Serbia was found legally responsible for failing to prevent or punish genocide committed by Bosnian Serb troops at the Srebrenica massacre.

Other UN tribunals have established genocide in only a handful of cases since the Holocaust, including Cambodia’s Khmer Rouge rule in the 1970s and the 1994 mass killings in Rwanda.

blocks.text: 2017 年 9 月，一名男子在孟加拉国纳夫河岸边帮助从缅甸越境而来的罗兴亚穆斯林难民下船。照片：Fred Dufour/AFP/Getty Images
2017 年 9 月，一名男子在孟加拉国纳夫河岸边帮助从缅甸越境而来的罗兴亚穆斯林难民下船。照片：Fred Dufour/AFP/Getty Images
世界最高法院裁定：缅甸对罗兴亚少数群体实施了种族灭绝行为
该判决结束了长达七年的法律较量，被视为应对最严重国家罪行的关键考验
世界最高法院裁定，缅甸近十年前在“清剿行动”中对其罗兴亚少数群体实施了种族灭绝行为。
国际法院（ICJ）此前从未认定一国对种族灭绝负有责任，这次判决结束了长达七年的法律较量，被视为应对最严重国家罪行的一次关键全球考验。
国际法院院长岩泽雄司在宣读判决时说：“法院完全确信，缅甸实施了……种族灭绝公约所涵盖的行为，意图毁灭缅甸罗兴亚人口中的相当一部分。”
2016 至 2017 年，缅甸军方的行动迫使逾 70 万以穆斯林为主的罗兴亚人逃往孟加拉国，难民抵达时讲述了屠杀成人与儿童、轮奸以及烧毁村庄的经历。
各国政府一直在焦急等待这项在联合国法院所在地荷兰海牙作出的裁决，部分原因是该裁定将为种族灭绝指控开创先例，尤其是针对以色列的高关注案件。
种族灭绝由 1948 年联合国公约在纳粹大屠杀之后加以定义，比战争罪更难证明，因为需要证明存在毁灭某一民族、族裔、种族或宗教群体的特定“意图”。
缅甸一案由穆斯林占多数的冈比亚代表缅甸幸存者提起。该案依据的是关于种族灭绝言论和“行为模式”的主张，表明在对若开邦的袭击中有摧毁该群体的企图，包括在人们逃离时开枪射击并阻止他们返回。
今年 1 月，国际法院举行闭门会议，听取从孟加拉国难民营前来的幸存者陈述。仍有超过 100 万罗兴亚人居住在那里——全球最大的难民定居点，而据估计，在佛教徒占多数的缅甸，剩余人数不足 60 万。

blocks.alt: Mumtaz Begum, a Rohingya refugee, in a pink headscarf with facial scarring from burns.

blocks.text: 蒙塔兹·贝古姆 2017 年摄于孟加拉国科克斯巴扎尔。缅甸图拉托利村遇袭后不久，她逃往孟加拉国。她说，军方烧毁房屋、轮奸妇女，并在她面前杀害了她的丈夫和儿子。照片：Allison Joyce/Getty Images
2017 年逃往孟加拉国的难民向《卫报》讲述了图拉托利村的一场屠杀，幸存者描述了针对平民的系统性枪击、万人坑，以及儿童被溺死在河中。卫星影像后来显示该村已被烧毁，它是人权调查人员分析并用以构建种族灭绝指控的几个村庄之一。
听证期间，冈比亚司法部长达乌达·贾洛向法庭表示，此案并非“关于晦涩的国际法问题”。
“这关乎真实的人、真实的故事和一群真实的人，”贾洛说。“缅甸的罗兴亚人。他们一直是毁灭的目标。”
法律专家视周四的判决为种族灭绝认定中性暴力问题的关键考验，因为该公约规定，此类罪行可包括意图“防止生育”的行为。调查人员表示，轮奸以及士兵残害女性生殖器的记述，是为阻止生育而有意且系统地实施的。
缅甸否认实施种族灭绝，并声称其行动针对的是实施游击式袭击的罗兴亚武装组织。缅甸军方以大规模“清剿行动”作为回应。
该国领导人敏昂莱在 2016 至 2017 年袭击期间掌管军方，国际刑事法院（ICC）已对其发出未决逮捕令，指控其反人类罪；与国际法院不同，国际刑事法院起诉的是个人而非国家。

blocks.alt: A Bangladeshi guard watches Rohingya refugees walking along a muddy path by water.

blocks.text: 在孟加拉国科克斯巴扎尔的帕朗卡利，数千名逃离缅甸的罗兴亚难民越境后沿着泥泞稻田行走，孟加拉国卫兵在一旁戒备。照片：Paula Bronstein/Getty Images
这位前将军在 2021 年政变中推翻了昂山素季的民选政府，引发内战，已造成数万人死亡。在广泛被认为缺乏公信力的选举之后，他于 4 月被立为文职总统。
尽管国际法院没有强制执行裁决的权力，但其决定被视为具有约束力，具有外交分量，并可影响包括制裁在内的国际行动。
以色列及其主要盟友美国一直在密切关注缅甸一案，因为该裁决最能暗示法官可能如何评估由南非提起的加沙案件。联合国独立调查以及种族灭绝学者已经表示，以色列在加沙实施了种族灭绝行为。
有预测称，认定缅甸违反该公约的判决将导致美国对国际法院法官实施制裁，其中包括今年的诺贝尔和平奖得主纳维·皮莱。

blocks.alt: A Myanmar border guard watches Rohingya refugees behind a barbed-wire fence.

blocks.text: 2018 年，一名缅甸边境卫队警察站在围栏附近，栏后是缅甸西部若开邦孟加拉国—缅甸边境“无人区”的罗兴亚难民和临时房屋。照片：Nyein Chan Naing/EPA
基于拜登政府的认定，华盛顿曾将罗兴亚危机视为种族灭绝。然而，特朗普政府一直在向国际人权机构发起攻势，包括对国际刑事法院实施制裁。
国际法院另外两起涉及 1990 年代巴尔干战争暴行的案件，未能认定有关国家须对种族灭绝直接负责，不过塞尔维亚被认定须为未能阻止或惩处波斯尼亚塞族军队在斯雷布雷尼察屠杀中实施的种族灭绝承担法律责任。
自大屠杀以来，其他联合国法庭仅在少数案件中认定种族灭绝，其中包括 1970 年代柬埔寨红色高棉统治，以及 1994 年卢旺达大屠杀。

items.title: Venezuela signs military deal with US less than a year after Maduro's removal
items.summary: The US Secretary of Defence says Venezuela has "gone from our most aggressive regional threat to a compliant security partner".
items.body:
Image source, Miraflores Palace/Handout via REUTERS

Image caption,

Pete Hegseth met Venezuela's interim president at the presidential palace

ByVanessa Buschschlüter

Latin America online editor

The United States and Venezuela have re-established military ties less than a year after US forces seized the then-leader of the South American country, Nicolás Maduro, in a raid on the capital, Caracas.

The interim government led by Delcy Rodríguez, Maduro's former vice-president, signed a military co-operation agreement with US Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth on Wednesday.

Few details about the deal have been released so far but Hegseth said that Venezuela had "gone from our most aggressive regional threat to a compliant security partner" in less than 12 months.

Interim President Rodríguez said the deal would help confront "common threats".

Military co-operation between the two countries was terminated in 2005 by Hugo Chávez, Venezuela's left-wing president at the time.

Chávez alleged that US military personnel sent to Venezuela to train their counterparts had made disparaging remarks about his government.

He also accused the US military office located in Fuerte Tiuna, Venezuela's largest military complex, of being "an organ of the CIA... conspiring against the government".

Under Nicolás Maduro, who succeeded Chávez after the latter's death from cancer, relations between the two countries deteriorated further.

They reached rock bottom late last year when the US doubled its reward for information leading to Maduro's capture to $50m (£38m) and eventually seized him on 3 January in a military raid.

Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, are now in custody in New York on charges of drug-trafficking and conspiracy to commit torture, which they deny.

Hegseth addressed the change in the two countries' relationship since Maduro was seized in his speech at the US embassy in Caracas on Wednesday.

"It's a great honour to be here as the first United States Secretary of War this century to set foot in Venezuela. The weight of this moment does not escape me," he said.

"Just one year ago, my presence here, our presence here would have been deemed impossible, almost unimaginable," he added before recalling a public appearance by then-President Maduro which had angered the Trump administration.

"Exactly one year ago today, the indicted narco-terrorist fugitive Nicolás Maduro, the man who spent more than a decade handing Venezuela's borders and territory to terrorists from all over the world, stood on a stage, not too far from here, and yelled mockingly: 'Come and get me!'. Well, we answered that call."

Image source, Juan BARRETO / AFP via Getty Images

Hegseth added that the result of the US military raid on 3 January had been as Maduro predicted, quoting the deposed leader's words: "No war, yes peace."

He described the deal signed by him and Venezuela's defence minister on Wednesday as a "new chapter for the United States, for Venezuela, for the Venezuelan military and for the Western Hemisphere through the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition".

Rodríguez described it as "extraordinarily relevant for our bilateral relations".

"In a matter of months, secretary, we have turned very difficult moments for our people into a space for co-operation and mutual benefit for both of our countries," she said addressing Hegseth during a meeting at the presidential palace.

While no details of the deal have been published, in her speech Rodríguez mentioned the training of Venezuela's armed forces and improving its "operational equipment" and access to new technology "to confront shared threats".

In his speech at the US embassy, Hegseth was more direct about who he considers to be those threats. Addressing "the narco-terrorists who abuse this [Venezuela] as a safe haven", he warned that "we will hunt you down, we will find you, and we will kill you".

From Venezuela, Hegseth travelled on to neighbouring Colombia, whose president, Abelardo de la Espriella, is a close ally of the Trump administration.

Colombia is already part of the US-led Americas Counter Cartel Coalition and in August, Hegseth had floated the possibility of joint US-Colombian military operations against armed groups.

On Wednesday, President de la Espriella took to X to deny a report by the New York Times which had stated that he had rejected carrying out joint operations, external.

In his post, he stressed that any decision would be taken while respecting Colombia's constitution, and the country's laws and sovereignty.

Hegseth reposted the tweet commenting that the US-Colombian partnership "is stronger than ever before".

items.title: What is at stake at the EU-UK summit in Brussels?
items.summary: Leaders will wrestle with easing Brexit red tape, restoring emissions trading and opening up youth mobility UK politics live – latest updates The EU and UK will hold a long-awaited summit in Brussels on Friday – the second since Brexit – to hammer out the UK’s longer-term relationship with the bloc.…
items.body:
Leaders at the Brussels summit will try to ease barriers to the cross-border trade of meat, cheese, wine and flowers. Photograph: Gareth Fuller/PA

Leaders at the Brussels summit will try to ease barriers to the cross-border trade of meat, cheese, wine and flowers. Photograph: Gareth Fuller/PA

Explainer

What is a stake at the EU-UK summit in Brussels?

Leaders will wrestle with easing Brexit red tape, restoring emissions trading and opening up youth mobility

• UK politics live – latest updates

The EU and UK will hold a long-awaited summit in Brussels on Friday – the second since Brexit – to hammer out the UK’s longer-term relationship with the bloc.

It will be attended by the prime minister, Andy Burnham, the head of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, and the president of the European Council, António Costa.

The gathering, which follows up last year’s inaugural EU-UK summit in London, was scheduled for July but postponed when Keir Starmer resigned.

What is on the table?

The two sides hope to announce three deals, which were launched under Starmer’s government.

First, a food and drink agreement that will remove a lot of Brexit red tape on animal and plant products, making it easier to trade meats, cheese, wine and flowers. To secure the deal, which is not expected to take effect until 2028, the UK will align with EU standards, meaning the government, for example, must abandon a planned ban on foie gras imports.

A second agreement will link the British emissions trading system with its bigger EU cousin, restoring a link severed by Brexit. It is a significant step for industry because EU and UK businesses will be exempt from each other’s charges on high-carbon imports such as steel, cement and electricity. This agreement also requires alignment with relevant EU rules.

The third deal is the most contentious: a youth mobility scheme that will give 18- to 30-year-olds the right to live, work, travel and study on both sides of the Channel for up to three years. The scheme may not be up and running until 2030 – bad news for anyone in their late 20s.

With less than 24 hours before the summit begins, two big issues remain open. EU negotiators want to ensure EU students pay the UK rate of university tuition, around four or five times lower than international fees. The two sides also disagree over how many people would be allowed to take part: the EU wants 100,000 visas a year, but the UK is looking at 50,000 to 80,000 to keep migration numbers down.

To maximise its leverage on tuition fees, the EU is linking the three agreements, warning they must enter force together.

EU negotiators want their students to pay tuition fees at UK levels instead of the much higher international rate. Photograph: Chris Ison/PA

Will the UK be included in Made in Europe?

Not on Friday. The UK has been pushing for inclusion in the EU’s Made in Europe plan, a protectionist scheme to favour EU companies when public money is being spent on goods such as electric cars, renewable energy and nuclear technology. Inclusion in Made in Europe is a big priority for the Burnham government, which has dangled major concessions on tuition fees to make sure British firms are not shut out.

The problem for London is that the EU lawmakers have not finalised the Made in Europe law, known as the Industrial Accelerator Act. Many EU member states want to include the UK, but France and the European parliament take a stricter position.

The EU law is not expected to be agreed until spring 2027. To help the British government, which has linked a generous offer on youth mobility with Made in Europe, the European Commission proposed delaying agreement on tuition fees by six months. But member states want precise guarantees now about equal treatment for EU students.

Another problem is that British inclusion in Made in Europe requires the UK to sign up to EU trade-defence policies. The EU, for instance, has imposed high tariffs on “unfairly subsidised” Chinese electric cars and fears the UK, which has not followed suit, could become an alternative route into the EU if Chinese companies set up in Britain and sell into the bloc. The EU is calling on the UK to align with its trade-defence policies, but the UK insists it can guard against circumvention without copying the EU.

In a sign of possible tensions, an earlier summit text proposing a trusted partnership on economic security has been downgraded to a partnership.

An agreement expected next year will bring the UK back into the EU’s internal electricity market. Photograph: CW Images/Alamy

What happens next?

Beyond the headline deals, the EU-UK draft summit statement opens the door to British integration in European policies on energy, crime-fighting, educational exchange, tech and foreign policy cooperation.

The next major agreement, targeted for next year, is bringing the UK back into the EU’s internal electricity market. This is a priority for five EU member states – Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands, Denmark and Luxembourg. They argue that Britain’s inclusion in the EU electricity market is essential to take advantage of the nascent green power boom in the North Sea. In return for market access, the UK will be required to contribute to the EU budget to aid the development of poorer EU regions.

Beyond that, the two sides will “explore opportunities” for the UK to join the Erasmus student exchange programme after 2027 – the current arrangement applies only for the 2027/8 academic year.

In a win for the UK, the EU appears ready to expand talks on the mutual recognition of professional qualifications, beyond existing negotiations on architects. The sides will sign a digital partnership, which includes joint work on AI safety. And examine how to share data on law enforcement and border management.

Is this joining the EU by the backdoor?

Far from it. A lot of diplomatic plates are spinning, but the UK remains outside the EU’s biggest economic clubs: the single market and the customs union. It also has no decision-making powers inside the EU.

Burnham says he will set out the long-term options for the future relationship after this week’s summit. “The hard Brexit we were given is not good enough for Britain,” he said on Monday in a major speech. But amid concerns among some cabinet ministers about reopening Brexit divides, the prime minister appears to be taking a more cautious approach. He said the process would take time and insisted that “at every stage the British people will be the boss”.

The EU has welcomed Britain’s interest in rejoining but is wary of a protracted negotiation that could be reversed by an anti-EU British government.

In an echo of the Brexit years, EU insiders say, once again, that it is up to Britain to define what it wants.

Inclusion in Made in Europe is a big priority for the Burnham government, which has dangled major concessions on tuition fees to make sure British firms are not shut out.

The problem for London is that the EU lawmakers have not finalised the Made in Europe law, known as the Industrial Accelerator Act. Many EU member states want to include the UK, but France and the European parliament take a stricter position.

The EU law is not expected to be agreed until spring 2027. To help the British government, which has linked a generous offer on youth mobility with Made in Europe, the European Commission proposed delaying agreement on tuition fees by six months. But member states want precise guarantees now about equal treatment for EU students.

Another problem is that British inclusion in Made in Europe requires the UK to sign up to EU trade-defence policies. The EU, for instance, has imposed high tariffs on “unfairly subsidised” Chinese electric cars and fears the UK, which has not followed suit, could become an alternative route into the EU if Chinese companies set up in Britain and sell into the bloc. The EU is calling on the UK to align with its trade-defence policies, but the UK insists it can guard against circumvention without copying the EU.
In a sign of possible tensions, an earlier summit text proposing a trusted partnership on economic security has been downgraded to a partnership.

blocks.alt: Electricity pylons and power lines silhouetted against a golden sky

blocks.text: An agreement expected next year will bring the UK back into the EU’s internal electricity market. Photograph: CW Images/Alamy
What happens next?

Beyond the headline deals, the EU-UK draft summit statement opens the door to British integration in European policies on energy, crime-fighting, educational exchange, tech and foreign policy cooperation.

The next major agreement, targeted for next year, is bringing the UK back into the EU’s internal electricity market. This is a priority for five EU member states – Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands, Denmark and Luxembourg. They argue that Britain’s inclusion in the EU electricity market is essential to take advantage of the nascent green power boom in the North Sea. In return for market access, the UK will be required to contribute to the EU budget to aid the development of poorer EU regions.
Beyond that, the two sides will “explore opportunities” for the UK to join the Erasmus student exchange programme after 2027 – the current arrangement applies only for the 2027/8 academic year.

In a win for the UK, the EU appears ready to expand talks on the mutual recognition of professional qualifications, beyond existing negotiations on architects. The sides will sign a digital partnership, which includes joint work on AI safety. And examine how to share data on law enforcement and border management.
Is this joining the EU by the backdoor?

Far from it. A lot of diplomatic plates are spinning, but the UK remains outside the EU’s biggest economic clubs: the single market and the customs union. It also has no decision-making powers inside the EU.

Burnham says he will set out the long-term options for the future relationship after this week’s summit. “The hard Brexit we were given is not good enough for Britain,” he said on Monday in a major speech. But amid concerns among some cabinet ministers about reopening Brexit divides, the prime minister appears to be taking a more cautious approach. He said the process would take time and insisted that “at every stage the British people will be the boss”.
The EU has welcomed Britain’s interest in rejoining but is wary of a protracted negotiation that could be reversed by an anti-EU British government.
In an echo of the Brexit years, EU insiders say, once again, that it is up to Britain to define what it wants.

解释性报道
布鲁塞尔欧盟-英国峰会的利害关系是什么？
领导人将艰难处理放松脱欧繁文缛节、恢复排放交易以及开放青年流动等问题

items: 英国政治直播——最新动态

blocks.text: 欧盟与英国将于周五在布鲁塞尔举行一场期待已久的峰会——这是脱欧以来的第二次——以敲定英国与欧盟的更长期关系。
与会者将包括首相安迪·伯纳姆、欧盟委员会主席乌尔苏拉·冯德莱恩，以及欧洲理事会主席安东尼奥·科斯塔。
这次会议是对去年在伦敦举行的首届欧盟-英国峰会的跟进，原定于 7 月召开，但在基尔·斯塔默辞职后被推迟。
桌上有什么？
双方希望宣布三项协议，这些协议是在斯塔默政府任内启动的。
首先是一项食品饮料协议，将取消动植物产品上大量脱欧繁文缛节，使肉类、奶酪、葡萄酒和花卉贸易更加容易。为达成这项预计要到 2028 年才生效的协议，英国将对齐欧盟标准，这意味着政府例如必须放弃原计划的鹅肝进口禁令。
第二项协议将把英国排放交易体系与更大的欧盟体系重新连接，恢复因脱欧而切断的联系。这对产业意义重大，因为欧盟和英国企业将互免对方对钢铁、水泥和电力等高碳进口征收的费用。该协议也要求与相关欧盟规则对齐。
第三项协议最具争议：一项青年流动计划，将赋予 18 至 30 岁的人在英吉利海峡两岸生活、工作、旅行和留学最多三年的权利。该计划可能要到 2030 年才能启动——对二十多岁后半段的人来说是个坏消息。
距峰会开始已不到 24 小时，两大问题仍未解决。欧盟谈判代表希望确保欧盟学生按英国本地大学学费缴费，大约比国际生学费低四到五倍。双方还在参与人数上存在分歧：欧盟希望每年 10 万个签证，而英国为了压低移民数字，考虑的是 5 万到 8 万。
为了在学费问题上尽量争取筹码，欧盟把三项协议绑在一起，警告必须同时生效。

blocks.alt: Three students in gowns and mortarboards at a graduation event

blocks.text: 欧盟谈判代表希望其学生按英国本地学费缴费，而不是高得多的国际生费率。照片：Chris Ison/PA
英国会被纳入“欧洲制造”吗？
周五不会。英国一直在争取被纳入欧盟的“欧洲制造”计划，这是一项保护主义安排，在用电车、可再生能源和核技术等商品的公共资金采购中优待欧盟公司。被纳入“欧洲制造”是伯纳姆政府的一大优先事项，该政府已在学费问题上抛出重大让步，以确保英国企业不被关在门外。
伦敦面临的问题是，欧盟立法者尚未敲定被称为 Industrial Accelerator Act 的“欧洲制造”立法。许多欧盟成员国希望把英国包括在内，但法国和欧洲议会持更严格的立场。
该欧盟立法预计要到 2027 年春季才会达成。为了帮助已把一项慷慨的青年流动提议与“欧洲制造”挂钩的英国政府，欧盟委员会提议将学费协议推迟六个月。但成员国现在就希望得到关于欧盟学生平等待遇的明确保证。
另一个问题是，英国被纳入“欧洲制造”要求其签署欧盟的贸易防御政策。例如，欧盟已对“受到不公平补贴”的中国电动汽车征收高关税，并担心尚未跟进此举的英国，可能在中国企业赴英设厂并向欧盟销售时，成为进入欧盟的替代通道。欧盟呼吁英国与其贸易防御政策对齐，但英国坚持可以在不照搬欧盟做法的情况下防范规避。
一个可能存在紧张的迹象是，早先峰会文本中提出的经济安全“可信伙伴关系”已被降级为“伙伴关系”。

blocks.alt: Electricity pylons and power lines silhouetted against a golden sky

blocks.text: 一项预计明年达成的协议将让英国重返欧盟内部电力市场。照片：CW Images/Alamy
接下来会发生什么？
除了这些头条协议外，欧盟-英国峰会声明草案还为英国融入欧洲在能源、打击犯罪、教育交流、科技和外交政策合作方面的政策打开了大门。
下一个重大协议以明年为目标，是让英国重返欧盟内部电力市场。这是五个欧盟成员国的优先事项——德国、比利时、荷兰、丹麦和卢森堡。他们认为，将英国纳入欧盟电力市场，对于利用北海刚刚兴起的绿色电力热潮至关重要。作为市场准入的交换，英国将被要求向欧盟预算缴费，以援助较贫困欧盟地区的发展。
除此之外，双方还将“探索机会”，让英国在 2027 年之后加入 Erasmus 学生交流项目——目前的安排仅适用于 2027/8 学年。
对英国来说是一场胜利：欧盟似乎准备扩大关于专业资格互认的谈判，超出目前仅针对建筑师的磋商。双方将签署一项数字伙伴关系，其中包括在 AI 安全方面的合作。并将研究如何共享执法和边境管理数据。
这是在走后门加入欧盟吗？
远非如此。不少外交议题同时推进，但英国仍处于欧盟最大的经济俱乐部之外：单一市场和关税同盟。它在欧盟内部也没有决策权。
伯纳姆表示，他将在本周峰会之后阐明未来关系的长期选项。“我们被给予的硬脱欧对英国来说不够好，”他周一在一次重要讲话中说。但鉴于部分内阁大臣担心重新撕裂脱欧分歧，首相似乎采取了更为谨慎的态度。他表示这一过程需要时间，并坚持“在每一个阶段，做主的都将是英国人民”。
欧盟欢迎英国有意重新加入，但担心谈判旷日持久，又可能被反欧盟的英国政府推翻。
欧盟内部人士表示，这又一次像脱欧年代那样，得由英国自己说清想要什么。

items.title: Putin vows 'far more painful' response to Ukraine's strikes on Crimean Bridge
items.summary: The bridge - a symbol of Russia's occupation of the Crimean Peninsula - suffered major damaged following a combined attack by Ukraine earlier this week.
items.body:
Figure caption,

Final moments before stretch of Crimean Bridge collapsed after Ukrainian attack

ByClaire Keenan

The Crimean Bridge has been attacked by Ukraine for the third time this week, a Russian official has said.

The Moscow-installed head of Crimea, Sergei Aksyonov, confirmed that traffic was temporarily suspended following another strike on the bridge connecting mainland Russia to occupied Crimea.

The critical bridge had already been hit twice earlier in the week resulting in severe damage and part of the bridge collapsing into the water.

The important infrastructure has long been targeted by Ukraine because of its significance as a logistical and symbolic asset to Moscow's war effort.

Image source, Reuters

Image caption,

A screengrab of the damaged Crimean bridge in the Kerch Strait on 17 November

It comes as Russian President Vladimir Putin meets US President Donald Trump and China's President Xi Jinping on Thursday for landmark talks in China.

Aksyonov confirmed the strike on the bridge in the early hours of Thursday via Telegram, adding that assessment of the damage was under way.

Meanwhile, Ukrainian sources have continued to issue air raid alert warnings overnight for districts just outside of the capital Kyiv.

At least three people were killed in a Russian drone attack on Odesa on Wednesday, according to the regional state administration. Officials described the attack as "brutal and deliberate... directly targeting people and their lives".

President Volodymyr Zelensky has called the initial strikes on the Crimean Bridge as an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making.

• Putin's Crimean Bridge partly collapses as Zelensky hails 'unprecedented' attack by UkrainePublished1 day ago

Ukraine used drones and missiles against it on 17 November which brought down a key section of the road.

That section of the double-arched, 12-mile bridge now lies on the seabed, brought down by an arsenal of Ukrainian long-range weaponry in a seven-stage operation culminating in a dramatic collapse.

In response, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has said the bridge "will be rebuilt, and it will be even better than before".

While Ukrainian forces have struggled to close the bridge for good, recent attempts have brought them closer to destroying the bridge's crucial road and rail route for Russian soldiers heading towards the front line.

Russian forces have also targeted key bridge crossings over the Dnipro River in Kyiv in recent days.

Russian strikes hit the Pivnichnyi (Northern) and Pivdennyi (Southern) bridges causing traffic closures, partial damage to the metro system and some power and water outages.

items.title: US consortium wins huge Kenya mining deal, beating Chinese rivals
items.summary: The Mrima Hill site is estimated to hold deposits of critical minerals worth more than $60bn (£45bn).
items.body:
Image source, Getty Images

Image caption,

The US is playing catch-up with China's dominance in critical minerals mining and processing across Africa (file photo)

ByRichard Kagoe

Reporting fromNairobi

A US-led consortium, Frontier Minerals, has won the tender to develop Kenya's Mrima Hill mining project, beating seven bidders, including companies from China and Australia.

The site is estimated to hold deposits of critical minerals worth more than $60bn (£45bn), including niobium, used in electric vehicles, aerospace and defence technology.

Frontier Minerals says its proposal aims to keep more of the economic benefits in Kenya through "processing and refining of minerals in-country".

The deal comes as Washington seeks greater access to Africa's minerals, aiming to strengthen US supply chains and compete with China.

Frontier Minerals brings together three US companies - Bunker Hill Mining Corp, American Resources Corporation and ReElement Technologies Corporation. The consortium combines expertise in mineral resource development, critical materials supply chains and advanced refining technologies.

A central part of its proposal is to develop mineral processing and refining capacity in Kenya. Brad Marnett from Frontier Minerals said the company wanted the country to capture more value from its mineral resources.

Mrima Hill is located in Kwale County, near Kenya's Indian Ocean coastline. The site covers about 390 acres of forest.

The prospect of mining in the area has raised concerns among local residents, who fear the project could damage the forest and threaten their ancestral heritage.

There are also questions over whether communities living near the site will benefit from the investment.

Marnett was keen to reassure Kenyans that they would benefit: "We intend to create lasting opportunities for Kenyan workers, businesses and the wider economy through capacity-building and targeted investment, while prioritising environmental management and performance."

The consortium must still obtain a prospecting licence and meet the necessary regulatory requirements before the project can proceed.

The tender decision has drawn objections from competing bidders.

Reuters news agency reports that two rival companies intend to challenge the selection, with Australia's RareX alleging that Frontier Minerals missed an earlier submission deadline.

Kenya's government has maintained that the process was open and transparent.

The project comes as US strives to secure alternative sources of critical minerals and reduce dependence on China, which dominates the processing of several key minerals.

Washington has been pursuing partnerships with mineral-rich African countries, including the Democratic Republic of Congo and Zambia, as it seeks to strengthen supply chains for industries ranging from electric vehicles to defence technology.

Kenya's mining ministry says the sector is an important part of its plans to diversify the economy beyond traditional sources of revenue such as tourism, agriculture and financial services.

translation.summary: 据估计，姆里马山矿区蕴藏的关键矿产储量价值超过 600 亿美元（450 亿英镑）。
translation.label: 机器翻译

blocks.alt: A yellow heavy-duty mining truck loaded with dark materials stands stationary at a mining site, with an expansive mine landscape in the background.

blocks.text: 图片来源：Getty Images
图片说明，
在非洲关键矿产的开采和加工领域，美国正试图追赶中国的主导地位（资料图片）
作者：Richard Kagoe
内罗毕报道
由美国主导的财团Frontier Minerals中标开发肯尼亚姆里马山（Mrima Hill）采矿项目，击败了包括来自中国和澳大利亚的企业在内的七家竞标者。
据估计，该地拥有价值超过600亿美元（450亿英镑）的关键矿产储量，包括用于电动汽车、航空航天和国防技术的铌。
Frontier Minerals表示，其方案旨在通过“在国内加工和精炼矿产”，让肯尼亚留住更多经济利益。
该协议出台之际，华盛顿正寻求更多地获取非洲矿产，以加强美国供应链并与中国竞争。
Frontier Minerals由三家美国公司组成——Bunker Hill Mining Corp、American Resources Corporation和ReElement Technologies Corporation。该财团汇集了矿产资源开发、关键材料供应链和先进精炼技术方面的专长。
其方案的核心之一是在肯尼亚发展矿产加工和精炼能力。Frontier Minerals的布拉德·马内特表示，公司希望该国能从其矿产资源中获取更多价值。
姆里马山（Mrima Hill）位于靠近肯尼亚印度洋海岸的夸莱郡，占地约390英亩森林。
该地区可能开展采矿，已引起当地居民担忧，他们担心项目会破坏森林并威胁其祖传遗产。
项目附近社区能否从这项投资中获益，也存在疑问。
马内特急于向肯尼亚人保证他们会从中受益：“我们打算通过能力建设和有针对性的投资，为肯尼亚工人、企业和更广泛的经济创造持久机会，同时优先做好环境管理与绩效。”
该财团仍须取得勘探许可证并满足必要的监管要求，项目才能推进。
此次招标决定已引起竞标对手的反对。
路透社报道称，两家竞争公司打算对这一评选结果提出质疑，澳大利亚的RareX指控Frontier Minerals错过了更早的提交截止日期。
肯尼亚政府一直坚称该流程公开透明。
该项目出台之际，美国正努力确保关键矿产的替代来源，并减少对中国的依赖——中国在多种关键矿产加工领域占据主导地位。
华盛顿一直在与刚果民主共和国和赞比亚等矿产丰富的非洲国家寻求合作，以加强从电动汽车到国防技术等行业的供应链。
肯尼亚矿业部表示，该行业是其经济多元化计划的重要组成部分，旨在使经济不再仅仅依赖旅游、农业和金融服务业等传统收入来源。
